blocks: I have obeyed your instructions, most blessed father Augustine; and would that I had done so as effectively as I did it gladly. Yet I am little troubled either way about the outcome, whether I have acted rightly or otherwise. For you have already laboured over that judgement, whether I could do what you were instructing; I am content with the testimony of obedience alone, if indeed I have adorned it with will and effort. For in the great house of a great father of a family, though there are many animals of different kinds useful in helping the household, the care of the dogs is not the least. To them alone is it given by nature to be eager of their own will for what they are trained for, and, through an inborn rule of obedience, to be held back only by the expectation of a disciplined fear, until they are sent off by a nod or a sign with leave to do it. For they have their own appetites, as much nearer to rational creatures as they excel the brutes: that is, to discern, to love and to serve. For, discerning between masters and strangers, they do not hate those they chase, but are zealous for those they love; and loving their master and his house, they keep watch not as if from a body fit by nature, but out of the conscience of an anxious love. Hence also, in a mystic sacrament in the Gospels, the Canaanite woman was not ashamed to say, and the Lord did not disdain to hear, that the little dogs eat the crumbs under their masters' table. The blessed Tobias too, following the angel as his guide, did not scorn to have a dog as his companion. So, bound to your love for all by a special love, I have willingly obeyed your will. For since my submission owes the deed to the command of your fatherhood, and all of it is yours, since it returns from you to you, I have rendered my work more abundantly in this one thing that is mine: that I did it gladly.

You had instructed me to reply to the empty-talking perversity of those who, strangers to the City of God, are called pagans from the crossroads and villages (pagi) of country places, or gentiles because they are wise in earthly things. Since they do not seek the future, and either forget or do not know the past, they nevertheless defame the present times as if they were beset by evils beyond the usual, for this reason alone: that Christ is believed and God is worshipped, while idols are worshipped less. You had instructed me, then, to set out in an orderly and brief book whatever I could find, in all the records of histories and annals that can be had at present, from the ages gone by, that was grievous with wars, or corrupted with diseases, or sad with famine, or terrible with earthquakes, or unusual with floods of water, or fearful with eruptions of fire, or cruel with strokes of lightning and the blows of hail, or wretched too with parricides and crimes. This above all because it was not fitting that your reverence, intent on completing the eleventh book against these same pagans (the ten rising rays of which, as soon as they were lifted up from the watchtower of the Church's brightness, shone over the whole world), should be occupied with a slight little work; and your holy son Julian of Carthage, a servant of God, was demanding that his request in this matter be satisfied, with the same confidence with which he had made it. I set to work, and first of all I was overwhelmed with confusion myself, for as I often reflected on it the disasters of the present times had seemed to me to have boiled over beyond measure. For I have found that past days were not only as heavy as these, but more terribly wretched by as much as they were further from the remedy of the true religion. So that by this inquiry it has rightly become clear that death, greedy for blood, reigned while the religion that would forbid bloodshed was unknown; that as this religion dawned, death was stunned; that death is shut in now that the religion prevails; and that death will be nothing at all when this religion alone shall reign. I except, of course, and set aside those last days at the end of the world, at the appearing of Antichrist or even at the conclusion of the Judgement, when the Lord Christ foretold through the Holy Scriptures, and by His own testimony too, that there would be distress such as there had never been before. Then, by the same measure that is now and always is, but in a plainer and heavier trial, the intolerable tribulations of those times will bring proof to the saints and destruction to the wicked.

blocks: Almost all men devoted to writing, among the Greeks as well as the Latins, who have spread abroad in words the deeds of kings and peoples to keep their memory long, have made the beginning of their writing with Ninus, son of Belus, king of the Assyrians. Though in their blind opinion they would have the origin of the world and the creation of men believed to be without beginning, they nevertheless define kingdoms and wars as having begun with him; as if indeed the human race had lived until then in the manner of cattle, and only then had awoken, shaken and roused as if to a new foresight. I, however, have determined to trace the beginning of men's misery from the beginning of man's sin, touching on only a few things, and those briefly. From Adam, the first man, to Ninus, the 'great' king as they call him, when Abraham was born, there are 3,184 years, which have been either passed over or not known by all the historians. From Ninus or Abraham to Caesar Augustus, that is to the birth of Christ, which was in the forty-second year of Caesar's rule, when peace was made with the Parthians, the gates of Janus were shut and wars ceased in the whole world, are reckoned 2,015 years, in which the leisure and business of all wore themselves out between those who did deeds and those who wrote them. Therefore the matter itself demands that I touch, as briefly as possible, a few things from those books which, speaking of the origin of the world, made the past credible by foretelling the future and by the proof that followed afterwards. Not that I would seem to press their authority on anyone, but because it is worthwhile to recall the common opinion that we share with all. First, because if the world and man are directed by divine providence, which is just as it is good; and since man, who because of the changeableness of his nature and the freedom of his choice is both weak and stubborn, ought to be governed with kindness when he is in need of help, and must be corrected with justice when he is unrestrained in his freedom: then whoever sees the human race through himself and in himself perceives that this world has rightly been exercised, from the beginning of man, by good and evil things in turn. Next, since we are taught that sin and the punishment of sin began from the first man himself. Further, since even these writers, beginning from the middle of time, though they nowhere mention what came earlier, have described nothing but wars and disasters (and what else are wars to be called but evils falling on one side or the other? And evils of this kind, as they were then and as they are now, in so far as they are, are without doubt either open sins or the hidden punishments of sins): what hinders us from laying open the head of the matter whose body they have set out, and from showing, even by the slightest account, that those earlier ages, which we show to have been far more numerous, endured similar miseries?

So, being about to tell of the conflicts of the human race from the founding of the world to the founding of the city, and from there to the principate of Caesar and the birth of Christ, from which time the empire of the world has remained under the power of the city, or even to our own days, as far as I am able to call them to knowledge, and being about to show, as from a watchtower, the world burning with evils in its various parts, set alight by the torch of greed, I think it necessary first to set out the very circle of the lands that the human race inhabits, as it was divided into three by our ancestors and then marked out by regions and provinces. So that, when the disasters of wars and diseases are shown in their places, the studious may gain knowledge not only of events and times but of places too.

blocks: Our ancestors laid down that the circle of the whole earth, surrounded by the border of the Ocean, was three-cornered, and called its three parts Asia, Europe and Africa; though some have thought there were two, that is Asia, and then Africa, which should be taken as part of Europe.

Asia, girdled by the Ocean on three sides, stretches across the whole region of the east. Towards the west, on its right, it touches Europe, which begins under the pole of the north; on its left it gives way to Africa; and below Egypt and Syria it has our sea, which we generally call the Great Sea.

Europe begins, as I have said, in the region of the north, at the river Tanais, where the Riphaean mountains, facing away from the Sarmatian Ocean, pour forth the river Tanais. It passes the altars and boundaries of Alexander the Great, set in the territory of the Rhobasci, and swells the Maeotic marshes, whose immense overflow enters the Euxine Sea widely near the city of Theodosia. From there long straits are sent out near Constantinople, until this sea that we call Our Sea receives them. In Spain the western Ocean is the boundary of Europe, above all where the Pillars of Hercules are seen at the islands of Gades and the tide of the Ocean is let into the mouth of the Tyrrhenian Sea.

Africa begins at the borders of Egypt and the city of Alexandria, where the city of Paraetonium lies, on this Great Sea that washes between all the regions and the lands in the middle. From there, through the places the inhabitants call Catabathmos, not far from the camp of Alexander the Great and above the lake Chalearzus, and then past the borders of the upper Auasitae, it runs crosswise through the Ethiopian deserts and touches the southern Ocean. The boundaries of Africa to the west are the same as those of Europe, that is the mouth of the strait of Gades. Its farthest limit is Mount Atlas and the islands they call the Fortunate.
And since I have briefly given the general divisions of the threefold world, I shall take care to mark out, as I promised, the regions of the parts themselves.

Asia has, at the middle of its eastern front, the mouths of the river Ganges in the Eastern Ocean. On the left it has the promontory of Caligardamana, below which, to the south-east, lies the island of Taprobane, from which the Ocean begins to be called Indian. On the right it has the promontory of Samara on Mount Imavus, where the Caucasus ends; below it, to the north-east, lie the mouths of the river Ottorogorra, from which the Ocean is called Seric.

Within these bounds is India, which has the river Indus on the west, which is received by the Red Sea, and the Caucasus mountain on the north; the rest, as I have said, is bounded by the Eastern and the Indian Ocean. It has forty-four peoples, not counting the island of Taprobane, which has ten cities, and not counting a great many other inhabitable islands.

From the river Indus, which is on the east, to the river Tigris, which is on the west, are these regions: Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Persis and Media, in mountainous and rugged country. These have the Caucasus mountain on the north, and on the south the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, and in their midst the chief rivers Hydaspes and Arbis. In them there are thirty-two peoples. But it is generally called Parthia, though the Holy Scriptures often call the whole of it Media.

From the river Tigris to the river Euphrates is Mesopotamia, beginning in the north between Mount Taurus and the Caucasus. To the south it is followed by Babylonia, then Chaldaea, and last Arabia Eudaemon, which stretches eastwards in a narrow tract of land between the Persian and the Arabian Gulf. In these there are twenty-eight peoples.

From the river Euphrates, which is on the east, to Our Sea, which is on the west, and from the north, that is from the city of Dagusa, which lies on the border of Cappadocia and Armenia not far from the place where the Euphrates rises, to Egypt and the farthest end of the Arabian Gulf (which stretches westward from the Red Sea, that is from the Ocean, towards the south in a long, narrow channel full of rocks and islands), the land is generally named Syria. It has the very large provinces of Commagene, Phoenicia and Palestine, not counting the Saracens and Nabataeans, whose peoples are twelve.

At the head of Syria is Cappadocia, which has Armenia on the east, Asia on the west, the Themiscyrian plains and the Cimmerian Sea on the north-east, and on the south Mount Taurus, below which lie Cilicia and Isauria as far as the Cilician Gulf, which faces the island of Cyprus.

The region of Asia, or, to speak properly, Asia Minor, except for the eastern part where it runs on towards Cappadocia and Syria, is surrounded on every side by sea: on the north by the Euxine Sea, on the west by the Propontis and the Hellespont, on the south by Our Sea. There is Mount Olympus.

Lower Egypt has Syria Palaestina on the east, Libya on the west, Our Sea on the north, and on the south the mountain called Climax, and Upper Egypt, and the river Nile. The Nile seems to come up from the shore of the Red Sea where it begins, at the place called the market of Mossylon; then, flowing for a long way westward and making in its middle an island named Meroe, it at last bends to the north and, swollen by its seasonal floods, waters the plains of Egypt. Some writers say that it has its source not far from Atlas and is at once swallowed up by the sands; then, after a short space, it overflows into a vast lake, and from there glides eastward, as far as the Ocean, through the Ethiopian deserts, and turning again to the left comes down to Egypt. It is indeed true that there is a great river of this kind, with such a source and such a course, and that it truly breeds all the monsters of the Nile. The barbarians near its source call it Dara; the other inhabitants call it Nuhul. But in the region of the peoples who are called Libyo-Egyptians, not far from the river that we said bursts out from the shore of the Red Sea, it is received into an immense lake and swallowed up; unless perhaps it pours out by a hidden passage into the bed of the river that comes down from the east.

Upper Egypt stretches a long way to the east. It has the Arabian Gulf on the north and the Ocean on the south. For on the west it begins from Lower Egypt, and on the east it is bounded by the Red Sea. There are twenty-four peoples there.
And since we have described the southern part of all Asia, it remains to set out the part that is left, from the east to the north.

The Caucasus mountain first rises between the Colchians, who are above the Cimmerian Sea, and the Albanians, who are by the Caspian Sea. Its ridge seems to be one as far as the farthest east, but it has many names; and many would have this same ridge believed to be that of Mount Taurus, because the Parcohatras, a mountain of Armenia lying between Taurus and Caucasus, is in truth thought to join Taurus with Caucasus. But the river Euphrates shows that this is not so: pouring out from the root of Mount Parcohatras and making for the south, it keeps the Caucasus on its left and shuts off Taurus on its right. So between the Colchians and the Albanians, where it also has its gates, it is called the Caucasus mountain; from the Caspian Gates to the Armenian Gates, or to the source of the river Tigris, between Armenia and Hiberia, the mountains are called Acroceraunian; from the source of the Tigris to the city of Carrhae, between the Massagetae and the Parthians, it is Mount Ariobarzanes; from the city of Carrhae to the town of Cathippi, between the Hyrcanians and the Bactrians, it is Mount Memarmali, where amomum grows, and the next ridge from it is called Mount Parthau; from the town of Cathippi to the village of Safris, between the Dahae, the Sacaraucae and the Parthyenes, it is Mount Oscobares, where the river Ganges rises and laser grows; from the source of the river Ganges to the springs of the river Ottorogorra, which are in the north, where the mountain-dwelling Paropanisadae live, it is Mount Taurus; from the springs of the Ottorogorra to the city of Ottorogorra, between the Hunnic Scythians and the Gandaridae, it is Mount Caucasus. The last, between the Eoae and the Passyadrae, is Mount Imavus, where the river Chrysorhoas and the promontory of Samara are received by the Eastern Ocean. So from Mount Imavus, that is from the foot of the Caucasus and the right-hand part of the east where the Seric Ocean stretches, to the northern promontory and the northern river, and from there along the Scythian Sea, which is on the north, as far as the Caspian Sea, which is on the west, and as far as the outstretched ridge of the Caucasus, which is on the south, there are forty-two peoples of Hyrcanians and Scythians, wandering widely because of the barren expanse of the land.

The Caspian Sea rises from the Ocean in the region of the north wind, and both its shores near the Ocean are held to be deserted and uncultivated places. From there it stretches southwards through long straits, until, broadening over great spaces, it is bounded by the roots of the Caucasus mountain. So from the Caspian Sea, which is on the east, along the coast of the northern Ocean to the river Tanais and the Maeotic marshes, which are on the west, along the shore of the Cimmerian Sea, which is to the south-west, as far as the head and the gates of the Caucasus, which are on the south, there are thirty-four peoples. But generally the nearer region is called Albania, and the farther, below the Caspian Sea and mountain, the land of the Amazons.
The bounds of Asia have been set out as briefly as possible. Now I shall travel with my pen over Europe, as far as is granted to the knowledge of man.

It begins at the Riphaean mountains, the river Tanais and the Maeotic marshes, which are on the east, and runs along the shore of the northern Ocean to Gallia Belgica and the river Rhine, which comes down from the west; then as far as the Danube, which they also call the Hister, which is on the south and, directed towards the east, is received by the Pontus. On the east is Alania, in the middle Dacia, where Gothia is too, then Germany, where the Suebi hold the greatest part. Of all these there are fifty-four peoples.
Now I shall set out whatever the Danube shuts off from the barbarian lands as far as Our Sea.

Moesia has the mouths of the river Danube on the east, Thrace on the south-east, Macedonia on the south, Dalmatia on the south-west, Histria on the west, Pannonia on the north-west, and the Danube on the north.

Thrace has on the east the gulf of the Propontis and the city of Constantinople, which was formerly called Byzantium; on the north part of Dalmatia and a gulf of the Euxine Sea; on the west and south-west Macedonia; on the south the Aegean Sea.

Macedonia has the Aegean Sea on the east, Thrace on the north-east, Euboea and the Macedonian Gulf on the south-east, Achaea on the south, and on the west-south-west the Acroceraunian mountains at the narrows of the Adriatic Gulf, which mountains face Apulia and Brundisium; on the west Dalmatia, on the north-west Dardania, on the north Moesia.

Achaea is surrounded by sea almost on every side. For it has the Myrtoan Sea on the east, the Cretan Sea on the south-east, the Ionian Sea on the south, the islands of Cephallenia and Cassiope on the south-west and west, the Corinthian Gulf on the north, and on the north-east a narrow ridge of land by which it is joined to Macedonia, or rather to Attica. This place is called the Isthmus, where Corinth is, which has not far away in Attica, to the north, the city of Athens.
Dalmatia has Macedonia on the east, Dardania on the north-east, Moesia on the north, Histria, the Liburnian Gulf and the Liburnian islands on the west, and the Adriatic Gulf on the south.

Pannonia, Noricum and Raetia have Moesia on the east, Histria on the south, the Pennine Alps on the south-west, Gallia Belgica on the west, on the north-west the source of the Danube and the frontier that separates Germany from Gaul between the Danube and Gaul, and on the north the Danube and Germany.

Italy lies stretched from north-west to south-east, having the Tyrrhenian Sea on the south-west and the Adriatic Gulf on the north-east. The part of it that is shared with and joined to the continent is blocked by the barrier of the Alps. These, rising from the Gallic Sea above the Ligurian Gulf, shut off first the territory of the Narbonenses, then Gaul and Raetia, until they are fixed in the Liburnian Gulf.

Gallia Belgica has on the east the frontier of the river Rhine and Germany, on the south-east the Pennine Alps, on the south the province of Narbonensis, on the west the province of Lugdunensis, on the north-west the Britannic Ocean, and on the north the island of Britain.

Gallia Lugdunensis, drawn out long and bent narrowly, half encircles the province of Aquitania. It has Belgica on the east, and on the south part of the province of Narbonensis, where the city of Arelate lies and the river Rhône is received by the Gallic Sea.

The Narbonese province, part of the Gauls, has the Cottian Alps on the east, Spain on the west, Aquitania on the north-west, Lugdunensis on the north, Gallia Belgica on the north-east, and on the south the Gallic Sea, which is between Sardinia and the Balearic islands; and in front of it, where the river Rhône goes out into the sea, it has the Stoechades islands.

The province of Aquitania is bent into a circle by the slanting course of the river Liger, which is for the most part its boundary. It has on the north-west the Ocean that is called the Aquitanian Gulf, on the west the Spains, on the north and east Lugdunensis, and on the south-east and south it touches the province of Narbonensis.

Spain as a whole is three-cornered in its position, and by the flowing round of the Ocean and the Tyrrhenian Sea it is made almost an island. Its first corner, facing the east, hemmed in on the right by the province of Aquitania and on the left by the Balearic Sea, fits into the territory of the Narbonenses. The second corner points north-west, where Brigantia, a city of Gallaecia, raises a very high lighthouse, a work worth recording among few, as a watchtower towards Britain. Its third corner is where the islands of Gades, facing south-west, look out over a gulf of the Ocean between them towards Mount Atlas.

Hither Spain, beginning from the east, is drawn by the Pyrenean forests on the northern side as far as the Cantabrians and Asturians, and from there through the Vaccaei and the Oretani, whom it has on the west, it is bounded by Carthago, set on the shore of Our Sea.

Farther Spain has the Vaccaei, Celtiberians and Oretani on the east, the Ocean on the north, the Ocean on the west, and on the south the Gaditan strait of the Ocean, through which Our Sea, which is called Tyrrhenian, is let in.
And since the Ocean has islands, which they call Britain and Hibernia, lying on the far side of the Gauls, facing Spain, they will be briefly set out.

Britain, an island of the Ocean, stretches a long way to the north; on the south it has the Gauls. Its nearest shore is opened to those who cross by a city called the port of Rutupiae; from there it looks out, not far from the Morini, towards the Menapii and Batavi lying to the south. This island is eight hundred miles in length and two hundred in breadth.
Behind it, where it opens on the boundless Ocean, it has the Orcades islands, twenty of which are deserted and thirteen inhabited.
Then the island of Thule, which, separated from the others by a boundless distance, lying in the middle of the Ocean towards the north-west, is known to scarcely a few.

The island of Hibernia, lying between Britain and Spain, stretches a long way from south-west to north-east. Its nearer parts, facing the Cantabrian Ocean, look far off, across a wide interval, towards Brigantia, the city of Gallaecia, which faces it from the south-west to the north-west, above all from the promontory where the mouth of the river Scena is and where the Velabri and Luceni live. This island is nearer to Britain, narrower in extent of land, but more useful for the mildness of its climate and soil; it is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots.
Next to it is also the island of Mevania, itself of no small size, and of fertile soil. It too is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots.
These are the bounds of all Europe.

Africa, as I have said, when our ancestors described it as to be taken as the third part of the world, they followed not the measures of its extent but the reasons of the division. For this Great Sea, which rises from the Ocean in the west and inclines more to the south, has made the bounds of Africa narrower, hemmed in between it and the Ocean. Asia, girdled by the Ocean on three sides, stretches across the whole region of the east. Towards the west, on its right, it touches Europe, which begins under the pole of the north; on its left it gives way to Africa; and below Egypt and Syria it has our sea, which we generally call the Great Sea. Europe begins, as I have said, in the region of the north, at the river Tanais, where the Riphaean mountains, facing away from the Sarmatian Ocean, pour forth the river Tanais. It passes the altars and boundaries of Alexander the Great, set in the territory of the Rhobasci, and swells the Maeotic marshes, whose immense overflow enters the Euxine Sea widely near the city of Theodosia. From there long straits are sent out near Constantinople, until this sea that we call Our Sea receives them. In Spain the western Ocean is the boundary of Europe, above all where the Pillars of Hercules are seen at the islands of Gades and the tide of the Ocean is let into the mouth of the Tyrrhenian Sea. Africa begins at the borders of Egypt and the city of Alexandria, where the city of Paraetonium lies, on this Great Sea that washes between all the regions and the lands in the middle. From there, through the places the inhabitants call Catabathmos, not far from the camp of Alexander the Great and above the lake Chalearzus, and then past the borders of the upper Auasitae, it runs crosswise through the Ethiopian deserts and touches the southern Ocean. The boundaries of Africa to the west are the same as those of Europe, that is the mouth of the strait of Gades. Its farthest limit is Mount Atlas and the islands they call the Fortunate. And since I have briefly given the general divisions of the threefold world, I shall take care to mark out, as I promised, the regions of the parts themselves. Asia has, at the middle of its eastern front, the mouths of the river Ganges in the Eastern Ocean. On the left it has the promontory of Caligardamana, below which, to the south-east, lies the island of Taprobane, from which the Ocean begins to be called Indian. On the right it has the promontory of Samara on Mount Imavus, where the Caucasus ends; below it, to the north-east, lie the mouths of the river Ottorogorra, from which the Ocean is called Seric. Within these bounds is India, which has the river Indus on the west, which is received by the Red Sea, and the Caucasus mountain on the north; the rest, as I have said, is bounded by the Eastern and the Indian Ocean. It has forty-four peoples, not counting the island of Taprobane, which has ten cities, and not counting a great many other inhabitable islands. From the river Indus, which is on the east, to the river Tigris, which is on the west, are these regions: Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Persis and Media, in mountainous and rugged country. These have the Caucasus mountain on the north, and on the south the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, and in their midst the chief rivers Hydaspes and Arbis. In them there are thirty-two peoples. But it is generally called Parthia, though the Holy Scriptures often call the whole of it Media. From the river Tigris to the river Euphrates is Mesopotamia, beginning in the north between Mount Taurus and the Caucasus. To the south it is followed by Babylonia, then Chaldaea, and last Arabia Eudaemon, which stretches eastwards in a narrow tract of land between the Persian and the Arabian Gulf. In these there are twenty-eight peoples. From the river Euphrates, which is on the east, to Our Sea, which is on the west, and from the north, that is from the city of Dagusa, which lies on the border of Cappadocia and Armenia not far from the place where the Euphrates rises, to Egypt and the farthest end of the Arabian Gulf (which stretches westward from the Red Sea, that is from the Ocean, towards the south in a long, narrow channel full of rocks and islands), the land is generally named Syria. blocks: When, after the making and adorning of this world, man, whom God had made upright and spotless, and so the human race, corrupted by its lusts, had grown filthy with sins, a just punishment at once followed an unjust licence. The sentence of God the creator and judge, laid down for sinning man, and for the earth because of man, and to last as long as men inhabit the earth, we all, unwilling though we may be, either prove by denying it or endure by confessing it; and their own weakness brands it as a witness on stubborn minds that Scripture has not faithfully persuaded. Next, the most truthful writers teach most plainly that when the sea was poured back over all the earth and the Flood let in, so that, with the whole world covered, there was one expanse of sky and sea, the whole human race was destroyed, a few being kept in the ark, by the merit of their faith, to replace its origin. That it happened has been attested even by those who, though they did not know past times nor the very author of time, nevertheless learned it by inference, from the evidence and the conjecture of the stones that we often see on remote mountains rough with shells and oysters, and often hollowed out by water. blocks: In the 1,300th year before the founding of the city Ninus, king of the Assyrians, the 'first' as they would have it, out of lust for extending his dominion, carried arms abroad and spent a bloody life of fifty years in wars throughout all Asia. Rising from the south and from the Red Sea, under the farthest north he subdued the Euxine Sea by laying it waste, and taught the Scythian barbarians, then still unwarlike and harmless, to rouse their sleeping savagery, to know their own strength, and to drink no longer the milk of cattle but the blood of men, and at last to conquer while being conquered. Last of all he crushed in battle and killed Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians and, they say, the inventor of the art of magic. Afterwards he himself, while he was attacking a city that had revolted from him, was struck by an arrow and died. When he was dead his wife Semiramis succeeded him, having a man's spirit and the dress of her son, and for forty-two years she exercised her peoples, already greedy from the practice of blood, in the slaughter of nations. Not content with the boundaries that she had received, acquired by her husband in fifty years when he was the only warrior then, the woman added to her empire Ethiopia, pressed by war and smeared with blood. She also made war on the Indians, whom no one but she and Alexander the Great ever entered. To pursue and slaughter peoples living in peace was crueller and heavier at that time than it is now for this reason: that among them then there were neither any fires of war abroad nor such great exercise of greed at home. This woman, burning with lust and thirsting for blood, amid unceasing debauchery and murders, used to kill all those whom she had summoned like a queen and kept like a harlot when she had enjoyed their embraces; and at last, having shamefully conceived a son, impiously exposed him and incestuously known him, she covered her private disgrace with a public crime. For she ordered that between parents and children, with no respect paid to nature, it should be free for each to seek marriage as they pleased.

blocks: In the 1,160th year before the founding of the city the region bordering Arabia, which was then called the Pentapolis, was utterly burned by fire from heaven, as Cornelius Tacitus too records among others. He speaks thus: "Not far from there are plains which they say were once fertile and inhabited by great cities, and were burned by the stroke of lightning; but that traces remain, and that the earth itself, solid in appearance, has lost its power to bear fruit." And though in this place, as if ignorant, he said nothing of the cities burned for the sins of men, a little later, as if forgetting his intention, he adds and says: "Just as I would grant that once famous cities blazed with fire from heaven, so I think that the earth is infected and corrupted by the exhalation of the lake." By saying this, though unwillingly, he openly confessed that he both knew and granted the burning of the cities, which without doubt were consumed by the guilt of their sins, and he plainly showed that it was not knowledge of the truth that he lacked but the will to express it. This will now be set out by me more fully.

On the border of Arabia and Palestine, where the mountains sent down on either side are received by the plains below them, there were five cities: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Zoar. Of these Zoar was small, the others large and great, for they had both a fertile soil beneath them and the river Jordan, spread over the plains and divided in convenient places, spent itself in increasing their richness. For this whole region, which used its goods ill, the abundance of things was the cause of its evils. For out of abundance grew luxury, and out of luxury foul lusts, so that males, working shame with males, rushed headlong without regard even to places, conditions or ages. So God in His anger rained fire and brimstone upon this land, and condemned the whole region, burned up with its peoples and cities, to eternal destruction, to be a witness of His judgement in time to come; so that even now the shape of the region indeed appears, but the region is found to be of ashes, and the sea poured over it now covers the middle valley that the Jordan had watered. And so much divine indignation was kindled over things that are thought small, that because those people, using their goods ill, had made the fruits of His mercies into the food of their lusts, the very earth too that had held these cities, first burned by fire and then overwhelmed by water, perished from the common sight into eternal damnation.

blocks: So now, if they please, let those who, as far as in them lies, spit at Christ, whom we have shown to be the judge of the ages, distinguish between the causes of Sodom and of Rome and compare the punishments. These I need not go over again, chiefly for this reason, that they are known to all. And yet how gladly I would accept their opinions, if they would confess faithfully what they feel. Though, since few murmur about the Christian times, and that in corners, I should not think it something to take so very hard, since the feeling and the speech of the whole Roman people has been made known with one voice and an equal judgement. It testified beyond all doubt that its habit of pleasures had hesitated only a little, through a small and slight disturbance, for it cried out freely: "If it got back the circus, nothing had happened to it"; that is, the swords of the Goths had done nothing at Rome if the Romans were allowed to watch the circus games. Unless perhaps, as is the way with very many at this time above all, who after long rest think even a small worry that arises an intolerable labour, they put these most merciful warnings, by which we are all at some time touched, above the punishments of others that they have heard and read. Them at least I warn about this very end of the Sodomites and Gomorrhaeans, so that they may learn and understand how God has punished sinners, how He can punish, and how He will punish.

blocks: In the 1,008th year before the founding of the city there was in Egypt first an unusual and wearisome plenty, and then a continuous and intolerable famine, which Joseph, a just and wise man, relieved by divine foresight. So the historian Pompeius and his abridger Justin teach, who among other things says: "Joseph was the youngest of his brothers. His brothers, fearing his outstanding talent, seized him and sold him to foreign merchants. Carried off by them to Egypt, when he had there learned the magic arts by his clever wit, he was soon very dear to the king himself. For he was most skilled in prodigies and was the first to found the understanding of dreams, and nothing of divine or human law seemed unknown to him; so much so that, foreseeing a barrenness of the fields many years ahead, he had gathered the harvests; and such were the proofs of his skill that his answers seemed to come not from a man but from a god. Joseph's son was Moses, whom, besides the inheritance of his father's knowledge, the beauty of his form also commended. But when the Egyptians were suffering from scab and leprosy, warned by an oracle, they drove him out of the borders of Egypt together with the sick, so that the plague should not creep to more." So Justin. But since this same Moses, whom these writers attest was wise and learned, has written of these things more fully and truly, as done by himself and his people, the ignorance of these writers must first be supplied by his credit and authority, which even they approve; and then the deceitful malice of the Egyptian priests must be refuted. They either, by cunning, which is more evident, tried to withdraw from memory the plain anger and mercy of the true God, by a confused account given piecemeal, so that they should not show, to the shame of their idols, that He was rightly to be worshipped by whose counsel, they would have taught, these evils were announced and by whose help they were avoided; or perhaps, to take it more indulgently, they forgot. For by the foresight of our Joseph, who was a servant of the true God and was piously and earnestly concerned for the creation of his Lord, they had abundance of grain, as priests; but, because they were false priests, they did not grieve with the others who were hungry. For truly, the one who is pleased forgets; the one who is grieved remembers. Yet though the histories and annals are silent, the land of Egypt itself declares itself a witness to the events of this time. Brought then under the king's power and restored to its cultivators, it pays to this day, from all its produce, an unceasing tax of a fifth part. So this great famine was under a king of the Egyptians of Diospolis named Amosis, at the time when Baleus ruled the Assyrians and Apis the Argives. Before the seven years of famine there were seven other years of plenty before them. Their abundance, which would perish as carelessly as it had been born richly, our Joseph by his skill gathered and stored, and he preserved all Egypt. He acquired all the money for Pharaoh and the glory for God, rendering with most just stewardship tribute to whom tribute, and honour to whom honour. He gathered the cattle, the lands and the property of all; and those who had sold themselves with their lands for the rate of the dole they received, he released on the agreed terms of a fifth part. Who would believe that this Joseph, whom God appointed for the Egyptians as the author of their preserved safety, so quickly fell out of their memory that a little later they bound his sons and his whole kindred to slavery, afflicted them with labours and struck them down with slaughter? Therefore it is no wonder if now too some are found who, when they have turned aside the sword hanging over their necks by holding out the Christian name, either disown or defame the very name of Christ, by which alone they are saved, and claim that they are burdened by the times of those by whose merits they are set free.

blocks: In the 810th year before the founding of the city Amphictyon reigned at Athens, third from Cecrops. In his times a deluge of waters swept away the greater part of the peoples of Thessaly, a few being saved by refuges in the mountains, above all on Mount Parnassus. In its neighbourhood Deucalion then held the throne; he received those who fled to him on rafts and cherished and fed them along the twin ridges of Parnassus; and so they say that the human race was restored by him. Then too Plato is witness that very many plagues and dreadful diseases raged in Ethiopia, almost to the point of desolation. blocks: In the 805th year before the founding of the city unspeakable evils and intolerable plagues fell upon the Egyptians, as Pompeius and Cornelius attest. Since both of them set out to tell this of the Jews, they have troubled me somewhat by their disagreement. For Pompeius, or Justin, speaks in this way: "When the Egyptians were suffering from scab and leprosy, warned by an oracle, they drove Moses out of the borders of Egypt with the sick, so that the plague should not creep to more. So, made leader of the exiles, he carried off by theft the sacred objects of the Egyptians; and the Egyptians, trying to recover them by arms, were forced by storms to return home." But Cornelius speaks of the same matter thus: "Most writers agree that when a wasting disease arose throughout Egypt, which disfigured the body, King Bocchoris, approaching the oracle of Ammon and asking for a remedy, was ordered to purge his kingdom and to carry off that race of men into other lands as hateful to the gods. When the crowd, sought out and gathered in this way, had been left in waste places, and the rest were benumbed with tears, Moses, one of the exiles, warned them to look for no help from gods or men, but to trust themselves to a heavenly leader, by whose help they had first driven off their present miseries." So Cornelius says that the Jews were driven out into the deserts under compulsion from the Egyptians themselves, and afterwards adds carelessly that they had driven off their miseries in Egypt by the help of their leader Moses. By this it is shown that some things that were vigorously done by Moses have been concealed. Likewise Justin asserts that Moses, driven out together with the people, stole the sacred objects of the Egyptians, and that the Egyptians, trying to recover them by arms, were forced back by storms and returned home. And he too has revealed something more, though not the whole, of what the other concealed. Therefore, since both have borne witness to that great leader Moses, let the events be set out from him, as they were done and spoken through him.

When the Egyptians were tormenting the people of God, that is the race of Joseph, by whose help they had been saved, crushed with slavery and labour, and were moreover compelling them by a cruel order to kill their own offspring, God commanded through Moses, His messenger, that His people be let go free to serve Him. When He was scorned He drove the stubborn with the harshest punishments, until, loaded and crushed by ten plagues, they at last forced those whom they had not wished to let go even to hurry. After the waters were turned into blood, bringing to those burning with thirst remedies heavier than the punishments; after the horrid filth of frogs creeping over all things clean and unclean; after the fiery gnats, which could be escaped nowhere as the whole air quivered; after the dog-flies, running about with horrid motions even through the inner parts of the limbs and bitterly inflicting torments as grievous as they were foul; after the sudden ruin and general slaughter of all the cattle and beasts of burden; after the boils bursting out and the running sores and, as they preferred to call it, the 'scab and leprosy' breaking out over all their bodies; after hail mixed with fire, trampling down men, herds and trees everywhere; after the clouds of locusts, which, when everything had been consumed, pursued even the very roots of the seeds; after darkness dreadful with phantoms, palpable in its thickness, deathly in its length; at last after the death, alike throughout all Egypt, of the first-born, and an equal storm of bereavement over all, those who had not yielded to God when He commanded yielded to Him when He punished. But soon, with the worst repentance, they dared to pursue those they had let go, and paid the last penalty of their wicked obstinacy. For their king drove the whole army of Egypt, furnished with chariots and horsemen, against the wanderers; we can guess its number chiefly from this one proof, that six hundred thousand men feared it and fled. But God, the protector of the oppressed and the avenger of the stubborn, suddenly divided the Red Sea, and, broadening the edges on each side, held up the sides of the stiffened waves, raised like a mountain, so that, drawn on by the hope of an unobstructed path, the pious entered a way of salvation they had despaired of, and the impious a pit of death they had not expected. So, while the Hebrews walked safely over the dry ground, the masses of standing water poured back behind them, and the whole multitude of Egypt was overwhelmed and killed with its king; and the whole province, already tormented before by the plagues, was emptied by this last slaughter. There still exist the most certain monuments of these deeds. For the tracks of the chariots and the ruts of the wheels are seen not only on the shore but also in the deep, as far as the sight can reach; and if they are disturbed for a time, either by chance or by curiosity, they are at once restored by divine power to their former appearance by the winds and waves: so that whoever is not taught the fear of God by zeal for the religion made known may be terrified by the example of the vengeance He has taken.

In these times too a heat so continuous and heavy blazed up that the sun, carried along paths out of its way, is said not to have warmed the whole world with heat but to have scorched it with fire; and the Ethiopian could not bear the fierce heat pressed on him, more than usual, nor the Scythian, unused to it. From this some, while they do not grant God His unspeakable power, searching for empty little reasons, have woven the ridiculous fable of Phaethon.

After the waters were turned into blood, bringing to those burning with thirst remedies heavier than the punishments; after the horrid filth of frogs creeping over all things clean and unclean; after the fiery gnats, which could be escaped nowhere as the whole air quivered; after the dog-flies, running about with horrid motions even through the inner parts of the limbs and bitterly inflicting torments as grievous as they were foul; after the sudden ruin and general slaughter of all the cattle and beasts of burden; after the boils bursting out and the running sores and, as they preferred to call it, the 'scab and leprosy' breaking out over all their bodies; after hail mixed with fire, trampling down men, herds and trees everywhere; after the clouds of locusts, which, when everything had been consumed, pursued even the very roots of the seeds; after darkness dreadful with phantoms, palpable in its thickness, deathly in its length; at last after the death, alike throughout all Egypt, of the first-born, and an equal storm of bereavement over all, those who had not yielded to God when He commanded yielded to Him when He punished. But soon, with the worst repentance, they dared to pursue those they had let go, and paid the last penalty of their wicked obstinacy. For their king drove the whole army of Egypt, furnished with chariots and horsemen, against the wanderers; we can guess its number chiefly from this one proof, that six hundred thousand men feared it and fled. But God, the protector of the oppressed and the avenger of the stubborn, suddenly divided the Red Sea, and, broadening the edges on each side, held up the sides of the stiffened waves, raised like a mountain, so that, drawn on by the hope of an unobstructed path, the pious entered a way of salvation they had despaired of, and the impious a pit of death they had not expected. So, while the Hebrews walked safely over the dry ground, the masses of standing water poured back behind them, and the whole multitude of Egypt was overwhelmed and killed with its king; and the whole province, already tormented before by the plagues, was emptied by this last slaughter. There still exist the most certain monuments of these deeds. For the tracks of the chariots and the ruts of the wheels are seen not only on the shore but also in the deep, as far as the sight can reach; and if they are disturbed for a time, either by chance or by curiosity, they are at once restored by divine power to their former appearance by the winds and waves: so that whoever is not taught the fear of God by zeal for the religion made known may be terrified by the example of the vengeance He has taken. In these times too a heat so continuous and heavy blazed up that the sun, carried along paths out of its way, is said not to have warmed the whole world with heat but to have scorched it with fire; and the Ethiopian could not bear the fierce heat pressed on him, more than usual, nor the Scythian, unused to it. From this some, while they do not grant God His unspeakable power, searching for empty little reasons, have woven the ridiculous fable of Phaethon.

blocks: Likewise in the 775th year before the founding of the city fifty parricides were committed in one night among the sons of the brothers Danaus and Aegyptus. Then Danaus himself, the contriver of such great crimes, driven from the kingdom he had acquired by so many outrages, withdrew to Argos. There, after the Argives had been shamefully persuaded into the crime, he drove from the throne Sthenelas, who had received him as an exile in need, and reigned himself. Then too there was in Egypt the cruel hospitality, and crueller religion, of Busiris, a most bloodthirsty tyrant, who used to offer the blood of innocent guests to the gods who shared in his crimes: a thing without doubt execrable to men, though I should like to see whether it seemed execrable to the gods themselves too. Then too parricide was joined to the incest of Tereus, Procne and Philomela, and a feast of unspeakable food more execrable than either was added, when, because of the stolen chastity and cut-out tongue of her sister, the mother killed her little son and the father ate him. In the same times Perseus crossed from Greece into Asia, and there tamed barbarian peoples in a heavy and long war, and at last, as victor, gave his name to the subject people: for from Perseus they were called Persians.

blocks: But I am now forced to confess that, for the advantage of keeping the end in sight, I am passing over very many things out of such a throng of the world's evils and shortening everything. For I could never pass through so dense a wood unless I sometimes flew over it with frequent leaps as well. For since the kingdom of the Assyrians lasted 1,160 years, through almost fifty kings, to Sardanapalus, and until that time almost never rested from making or receiving wars, what end will be found if we try to recount them by numbering them, not to say by describing them? Above all since the matters of the Greeks must not be passed over, and those of the Romans must above all be reviewed. Nor is there any need for me now to enumerate the shameful deeds of Tantalus and Pelops and the more shameful fables. Of these, Tantalus, king of the Phrygians, when he had most shamefully carried off Ganymede, the son of Tros, king of the Dardanians, kept him with a greater foulness of the struggle that followed, as the poet Phanocles confirms, who records that a very great war was stirred up over this; or else because he would have this same Tantalus, as an attendant of the gods, be thought to have prepared the stolen boy for the lust of Jupiter by a household pandering, the man who did not hesitate to set his own son Pelops too before Jupiter's feast. It is wearisome too to tell of the contests of Pelops himself against Dardanus and the Trojans, however great, which, because they are commonly celebrated in fables, are listened to rather carelessly. I pass over those things too which are told, in Palaephatus's writing, of Perseus, Cadmus, the Thebans and the Spartans, through the inextricable recurrences of alternating evils. I keep silent about the outrages of the Lemnian women; I pass by the lamentable flight of Pandion, king of the Athenians; I say nothing of the hatreds, debaucheries and parricides of Atreus and Thyestes, hateful even to heaven. I leave out Oedipus, the killer of his father, husband of his mother, brother of his sons, stepfather to himself. I prefer to keep silent that Eteocles and Polynices laboured in mutual combat so that neither of them should fail to be a parricide. I do not wish to recall Medea, "wounded by cruel love" and rejoicing in the slaughter of her little children, and whatever was done in those times. It can be guessed how men endured what even the stars are said to have fled from.

blocks: In the 560th year before the founding of the city there was a most savage contest between the Cretans and the Athenians, in which, after the peoples on both sides had been unhappily struck down, the Cretans exercised a bloodier victory. blocks: In the 480th year before the founding of the city Vesozes, king of Egypt, eager either to mix in war or to join in a kingdom the south and the north, regions separated by almost the whole sky and sea, was the first to declare war on the Scythians, having first sent envoys to tell the enemy the terms of obedience. To these the Scythians replied to the envoys that a very wealthy king had foolishly taken up war against the poor, a war that he himself should rather have feared, the other way round, because of the uncertain outcome of war, with no rewards and plain losses. Further, they said they would not wait to be come to, but would go of their own accord to meet their booty. Nor was there any delay, for deeds followed the words. First they forced Vesozes himself, terrified, to flee back into his kingdom, and then they attacked the army he had abandoned and seized all the equipment of war; and they would have laid waste all Egypt too had they not been driven back, hindered by the marshes. Then, returning at once, they subdued Asia with endless slaughter and made it tributary. There they stayed fifteen years without peace, until at last they were called back by the insistence of their wives, who declared that unless they returned they would seek offspring from their neighbours.

blocks: Meanwhile among the Scythians two young men of the royal house, Plynos and Scolopetius, driven from home by a faction of the nobles, drew a great body of youth with them and settled on the coast of Pontic Cappadocia near the river Thermodon, with the Themiscyrian plains subject to them. There, after long plundering all that was nearest, they were massacred by an ambush through a conspiracy of their neighbours. Their wives, stirred by exile and widowhood, took up arms; and so that all might have an equal spirit from a like condition, they killed the men who had survived, and, inflamed against the enemy with their own blood, they achieved vengeance for their slain husbands by the destruction of their neighbours. Then, having won peace by arms, they took foreign men to their beds. The males that were born they soon killed; the females they brought up with care, burning off the right breasts of the infants so that the shooting of arrows should not be hindered; hence they were called Amazons. They had two queens, Marpesia and Lampeto, who divided their host into two parts and took by lot in turn the care of war and the guarding of home. So when they had subdued Europe for the most part, and had taken a good many cities of Asia, and had themselves founded Ephesus and other cities, they called home the chief part of their army, loaded with very rich booty; the rest, left to protect the rule of Asia, were massacred with Queen Marpesia by an onset of the enemy. Her place was taken by her daughter Sinope, who crowned a singular glory of valour with perpetual virginity. So great an admiration and dread had seized the peoples, roused by this fame, that Hercules too, when he had been ordered by his master to bring the queen's arms, as if destined to an inescapable danger, gathered all the chosen and noble youth of Greece and prepared nine long ships; and yet, not content with this swarm of strength, he preferred to attack unexpectedly and to surround them when they did not expect it. Two sisters were then at the head of the kingdom, Antiope and Orithyia. Hercules, carried by sea, overwhelmed them while they were off their guard and unarmed and idle through the carelessness of peace. Among the very many killed and captured, two sisters of Antiope were held, Melanippe by Hercules and Hippolyte by Theseus. But Theseus took Hippolyte in marriage, while Hercules returned Melanippe to her sister and took the queen's arms as the price of her ransom. After Orithyia, Penthesilea gained the throne, of whose valour among men in the Trojan War we have received the most famous proofs.

blocks: Oh, the pity of it, the shame of human error! Women who were fugitives from their country entered, roamed through and laid waste Europe and Asia, that is the greatest and strongest parts of the world, and held them for almost a hundred years, overthrowing very many cities and founding others: and yet it was not counted as a misery of men in the pressure of the times. But now the famous Getae, who are now the Goths too, whom Alexander declared to be avoided, whom Pyrrhus dreaded, whom Caesar too turned aside from, having left and emptied their own homes, entering the Roman provinces all together with all their strength, and long shown off together for terror, hope by entreaty for the alliance of a Roman treaty, which they could have claimed by arms. They ask for a seat of small habitation, not by their own choice but by our judgement, though the whole earth lay subject and open to them and it was free to them to take as much as they pleased. They offer themselves for the protection of the Roman realm, they whom alone unconquered kingdoms feared. And yet blind heathendom, since it does not see these things done by Roman valour, does not believe that they were obtained by the faith of the Romans, nor does it acquiesce, though it understands it, to confess that by the kindness of the Christian religion, which joins a kindred faith through all peoples, those men have been made subject to it without battle whose women destroyed the greater part of the earth with immense slaughter.

blocks: Then, in the 430th year before the founding of the city, there is told the rape of Helen, the conspiracy of the Greeks and the gathering of a thousand ships, then the ten-year siege and at last the famous destruction of Troy. In that war, waged most bloodily for ten years, what nations and how great peoples the same whirlwind caught up and struck down, Homer, a poet famous above all, has made plain in a most splendid poem; nor is it our business now to go over it again in order, for it seems both long for this work and known to all. Yet let those who have learned of the length of that siege, the cruelty of the overthrow, the slaughter and the captivity, see whether they are rightly offended at the present state of the times, whatever it is: when enemies whom, by the hidden mercy of God, they might have to pursue in war over all lands with armies drawn up, they follow over all seas for the sake of peace, holding out hostages; and so that they should not be thought to do this, perhaps, out of love of quiet, these offer themselves and their own dangers for the peace of the Romans against other peoples.

blocks: In the 64th year before the founding of the city Sardanapalus reigned last among the Assyrians, a man more corrupt than a woman. Seen among herds of harlots in a woman's dress, handling purple on the distaff, by his prefect Arbatus, who was then over the Medes, he was held in execration; soon he was also challenged to war when the peoples of the Medes were roused, and when he was defeated he threw himself on a burning pyre. From then the kingdom of the Assyrians passed to the Medes. Then, with many battles springing up on every side, which it seems in no way fitting to discuss in order, through various fortunes it passed to the Scythians and Chaldaeans and returned again by a like road to the Medes. In this brevity it must be weighed how great were the ruins and disasters of peoples, how many wars flowed, where so many and such kingdoms were so often changed. After this Phraortes ruled the Medes, who spent the twenty-two years of his reign in very frequent wars with the Assyrians and the Persians. After him reigned Diocles, a man most experienced in arms and always busy with wars, who at his death gave the empire, widely increased, to Astyages. Astyages, having no male offspring, had a grandson, Cyrus, born among the Persians. But Cyrus, as soon as he grew up, gathered a band of Persians and declared war on his grandfather. Astyages, forgetting the crime he had once committed against Harpalus, when he killed his only son, a little child, and set him before the father to feast on, and, so that no happy ignorance should take anything from that most unhappy bereavement, reproached the father with the infamous feast by showing him the head and hands: forgetful, then, of this deed, he entrusted the chief command of the war to Harpalus himself, who at once handed over the army he had received to Cyrus by treachery. When he learned this Astyages, taking forces with him, set out himself against the Persians and renewed the contest more fiercely, with a threat to his men that if anyone tried to withdraw from the battle he would be met with the sword. Since the Medes fought hard under this necessity, the line of the Persians was again driven back; and as it was gradually giving way, their mothers and wives ran to meet them and begged them to return to the battle. When they hesitated, the women lifted their clothes and showed the shameful parts of the body, asking whether they wished to flee back into the wombs of their mothers or wives. Blushing at this, they returned to the battle, and making a charge they forced those they had been fleeing to flee. Then Astyages was captured there; Cyrus took nothing from him but his kingdom, and put him over the very great people of the Hyrcanians. He himself did not wish to return to the Medes. This was the end of the empire of the Medes. But the cities that had been tributary to the Medes revolted from Cyrus, and this was the cause and origin of many wars for Cyrus.

blocks: At that time Phalaris of Sicily, having seized a tyranny, was ravaging the people of Agrigentum. Cruel in mind, crueller in his devices, doing everything wickedly against the innocent, the unjust man once found someone whom he punished justly. For a certain Perillus, a worker in bronze, seeking the tyrant's friendship and thinking it a gift fit for his cruelty, made a bronze bull, in whose side he skilfully set a door to serve as a way in for thrusting the condemned inside: so that when someone shut in there was roasted with fires set beneath, the hollow bronze, by its capacity, would increase the sound of the voice forced from him and, with a deathly beat, would give out a murmur suited to the image, and in this wicked spectacle it would seem the lowing of a beast and not the groaning of a man. But Phalaris, embracing the deed and cursing its maker, provided matter both for vengeance and for cruelty: for he punished the craftsman himself with his own invention.

There had also been, a little earlier, a king among the Latins, Aremulus, who for eighteen years grew in outrages and impieties, and at last, cut off by a thunderbolt by divine judgement, paid a ripe punishment at an unripe age.

In the 20th year before the founding of the city the Lacedaemonians, warring against the Messenians with untiring fury for twenty years because their maidens had been slighted at a solemn sacrifice of the Messenians, entangled the whole strength of Greece in their own ruin. They had devoted themselves with great curses and bound themselves with oaths never to return home unless Messene were taken by storm; and after ten years, worn out by the long siege and yet having gained no fruit of victory, they were being called back, moved besides by the complaints of their wives protesting at their long widowhood and the danger of barrenness. Holding a council, they feared that, with the hope of offspring cut off, this perseverance was breeding destruction for themselves more than for the Messenians. So they sent back to Sparta those chosen men in the army who had come as reinforcements after the oath was sworn, and allowed them to lie with all the women indiscriminately: a licence infamous enough, and yet not useful. They themselves, holding to their purpose, took the Messenians by a trick, and pressed the conquered into slavery. But the Messenians, after long enduring a bloody domination among blows and chains, shook off the yoke, took up arms and renewed the war. The Lacedaemonians chose Tyrtaeus, an Athenian poet, as their leader in battle. Routed in three encounters, they made good their lost army by calling a band of slaves to freedom. But when even so they thought that they should give up the contest for fear of danger, they were fired again by a poem composed by Tyrtaeus, their poet and general, and recited before the assembly, and they soon rushed into battle; and they met with such force of spirit that rarely has a bloodier battle ever blazed up. In the end, however, the victory was the Lacedaemonians'. A third time the Messenians renewed the contest. Nor did the Lacedaemonians delay. Both sides brought many forces as auxiliaries. The Athenians, for their part, prepared to attack the Lacedaemonians from the other side while they were busy elsewhere. Nor were the Lacedaemonians idle: for, being occupied with the Messenians themselves, they sent in the Peloponnesians to meet the Athenians in battle. The Athenians, having sent a small fleet to Egypt, were unequal in strength and were easily beaten in a naval encounter. Then, when their fleet had been recovered and they had been strengthened too by a force of soldiers, they challenged the victors to battle. The Lacedaemonians too left the Messenians and turned their arms against the Athenians. For a long time there were varied and heavy fights and a doubtful state of victory, and at last both sides withdrew with the outcome undecided. It must above all be known, however, that Sparta is the same city as Lacedaemon, and that from this the Lacedaemonians are called Spartans. So the Lacedaemonians, called back from there to the Messenian war, so as not to leave the time between idle for the Athenians, made a pact with the Thebans that they would restore to them the leadership of the Boeotians, which they had lost in the times of the Persian War, if they would take up the war with the Athenians. So great was the fury of the Spartans that, though entangled in two wars, they did not refuse to take up a third, provided that they could find enemies for their foes. The Athenians, disturbed by so great a storm of wars, chose two generals: Pericles, a man of proven valour, and Sophocles, the writer of tragedies. They divided the army, laid waste the territory of the Spartans far and wide, and added many cities of Asia to the empire of the Athenians. From then on, for fifty years, they fought on land and sea with victory always uncertain, until the Spartans, with their wealth diminished and their good faith ruined, became a disgrace even to their allies.

But that these things weighed on Greece through so many volumes of ages is thought of little account. Now, however, it is not borne that pleasures should sometimes be interrupted and lusts hindered for a little. Yet there is this difference between the men of that time and those of this one: that they bore these unbearable things with an even mind, because they had been born or brought up in them and had known nothing better; while these, accustomed all their lives to an unbroken clear sky of calm and delights, are disturbed by every cloud of worry, however slight, that gathers. And would that they would pray to Him who drives away even this slight disquiet, by whose gift they have had this continuity of peace unknown in other times. And since I remember that I promised, when I marked out the order of my telling as if by certain joints, to speak from the founding of the world to the founding of the city, let this be the end of this volume, which we have unfolded from the founding of the world, so that the following book may begin from the founding of the city. It will contain the evils of those times, more closely woven, since men were by then better practised and better schooled in wickedness.

blocks: I think there is no longer any man from whom it can be hidden that God made man in this world. Hence too, when man sins, the world is reproved, and to restrain our intemperance this earth on which we live is chastised by the failing of the other animals and the barrenness of its fruits. So if we are God's creatures, we are rightly God's charge too. For who loves more than He who made? And who rules in better order than He who both made and loves? And who can order and rule what is made more wisely and more strongly than He who both foresaw what was to be made and accomplished what He foresaw? Therefore those who have not read perceive, and those who have read recognise, that all power and every ordering is from God. And if powers are from God, how much more are kingdoms, from which the other powers proceed; and if kingdoms are various, how much more fittingly is there some greatest kingdom, to which the whole power of the other kingdoms is subject: such as was in the beginning the Babylonian, and then the Macedonian, afterwards too the African, and at the end the Roman, which remains to this day. And by the same unspeakable ordering, at the four cardinal points of the world, the leaderships of four kingdoms stand out in distinct degrees: the Babylonian kingdom in the east, the Carthaginian in the south, the Macedonian in the north and the Roman in the west. Between the first and the last of these, that is between the Babylonian and the Roman, as if between an old father and a little son, the African and the Macedonian came in, brief and in the middle, as if guardian and trustee, admitted by the power of the time and not by the right of inheritance. Whether this is so, I shall take care to set out most plainly.

blocks: The first king among the Assyrians who was able to stand out above the rest was Ninus. When Ninus was killed his wife Semiramis, queen of all Asia, restored the city of Babylon and made it the capital of the kingdom for the Assyrians. The kingdom of the Assyrians stood a long time with its power unshaken; but when Arbatus, whom others call Arbaces, prefect of the Medes and a Mede by nation, had killed his king Sardanapalus at Babylon, he transferred the name and the sum of the kingdom to the Medes. So the kingdom of Ninus and of Babylon was diverted to the Medes in the very year in which Procas began to reign among the Latins, the father of Amulius and Numitor and the grandfather of Rhea Silvia, who was the mother of Romulus. And so that I may show thoroughly that all these things were arranged by unspeakable mysteries and by the deepest judgements of God, and did not happen either by human strength or by uncertain chance: all ancient histories begin from Ninus, and all Roman histories arise from Procas. Then, from the first year of the rule of Ninus until Babylon began to be restored by Semiramis, sixty-four years passed; and from the first year of Procas, when he began to reign, to the founding of the city by Romulus, there were likewise sixty-four years. So in the reign of Procas the seed of the future Rome was sown, though no shoot yet appeared. In the same year of the reign of this Procas the kingdom of Babylon failed, though Babylon itself still stood. When Arbatus left for the Medes, the Chaldaeans kept part of the kingdom in their own hands and claimed Babylon for themselves against the Medes. So the power over Babylonia was with the Medes, the ownership with the Chaldaeans; but the Chaldaeans, because of the ancient dignity of the royal city, preferred to call themselves its people rather than call it theirs. So it came about that Nebuchadnezzar and the other kings after him down to Cyrus, though they are read of as powerful with the strength of the Chaldaeans and famous with the name of Babylonia, are nevertheless not counted in the number and at the turning point of the illustrious kings. So Babylon was dishonoured under the prefect Arbatus in the same year in which Rome, to speak properly, was sown under King Procas. Babylon was at last overthrown by King Cyrus at the very time when Rome was first freed from the domination of the Tarquin kings. For in one and the same correspondence of times the one fell and the other rose: the one then first suffered the domination of foreigners, the other then first scorned even the arrogance of its own rulers; the one then, as if dying, left its inheritance, and the other, coming of age, then recognised itself as heir; then the empire of the east set and that of the west rose.
And not to delay longer with words, I commit myself to the teeth of the raving, but to be set free by the protection of the truth.

blocks: Ninus reigned fifty-two years. He was succeeded, as I have said, by his wife Semiramis, who herself reigned forty-two years and in the middle of her rule founded Babylon as the capital of the kingdom. So Babylon, about 1,164 years after it was founded, was despoiled of its wealth and its kingdom, and deprived of its king himself, by the Medes and by Arbatus, their king but its own prefect; yet it remained unharmed itself for some while afterwards. Likewise Rome too, after the same number of years, that is about 1,164, was broken into by the Goths and Alaric their king, though its own count, and despoiled of its wealth, not of its rule; it still remains and reigns unharmed. Yet the order of the whole correspondence between the two cities has been kept by hidden decrees to such a degree that there its prefect Arbatus seized the kingdom, and here its prefect Attalus tried to reign: though in this city alone the profane attempt was made void by the merit of a Christian emperor.

So I have thought these things should be recalled above all for this reason: that, with so much of the unspeakable judgements of God laid open in part, those who murmur so foolishly about the Christian times may understand that one God has ordered the times, both for the Babylonians in the beginning and for the Romans at the end; that it is of His mercy that we live, and of our own intemperance that we live wretchedly. See, the rise of Babylon and of Rome is alike, the power alike, the greatness alike, the times alike, the goods alike, the evils alike; and yet the end is not alike, nor the failing. For the one lost its kingdom, the other keeps it; the one was bereaved by the killing of its king, the other is secure with its emperor unharmed. And why so? Because there the foulness of lust was punished in the king; here the most self-restrained justice of the Christian religion was kept in the king. There, without reverence for religion, the licence of fury satisfied the greed for pleasure; here there were Christians who spared, Christians whom they spared, and Christians for whose memory and in whose memory there was sparing. Therefore let them stop tearing at religion and provoking the patience of God, through which they have it that even this may go unpunished, if at some time they stop. Let them indeed recall with me the times of their ancestors, most restless with wars, execrable with crimes, foul with dissensions, most continuous in miseries: which they may rightly shudder at because they were, and must needs pray that they may not be; and pray indeed to the one God alone, who then by a hidden justice allowed them to happen, and now by an open mercy grants that they do not. These will now be set out by me more fully from the very beginning of the City, with the histories unrolled in order.
