blocks: In the 414th year after the overthrow of Troy, and in the sixth Olympiad (which is held, with a contest and games, at Elis, a city of Greece, every fifth year, four years being completed between), the city of Rome was founded in Italy by the twins Romulus and Remus as its founders. Romulus at once stained its kingship with parricide, and with a like success of cruelty he took the Sabine women, seized against all custom, bound them in wicked marriages and endowed them with the blood of their husbands and parents. So Romulus, having first killed his grandfather Numitor and then his brother Remus, seized the rule and established the city; he dedicated the kingdom with the blood of his grandfather, the walls with that of his brother, the temple with that of his father-in-law; he gathered a band of criminals by a promise of impunity. His first field for war was the forum of the city, a sign that wars foreign and civil, mixed together, would never be lacking. The women of the Sabines, whom he had enticed by a treaty and games, he seized as dishonourably as he defended them wickedly. Their leader Titus Tatius, an old man pressing honourable claims of piety, was long driven off by arms, and as soon as Romulus had taken him into partnership in the kingdom, he killed him. A battle was fought with the Veientes, then still of small name but already of great strength. The town of the Caeninenses was taken and destroyed. Once arms had been taken up there was never rest, since a foul want and a shameful hunger at home would be feared if they ever settled into peace. From here I shall touch as briefly as possible on the unceasing contests, always heavy in proportion to their strength: that Tullus Hostilius, the founder of military affairs, in his confidence in a well-trained youth made war on the Albans, and after long uncertain hope on both sides, and certain disaster, at last ended the worst outcomes and doubtful results by the short-cut of the combat of the triplets; that when the peace was broken again Mettus Fufetius, wavering in the Fidenate war and even planning treachery, paid the penalty of his double mind with a divided body, chariots tearing him in opposite directions; that the Latins often met Ancus Marcius as their enemy in battle and were sometimes overcome; that Tarquinius Priscus cut down in countless encounters all his neighbours and the twelve peoples of Etruria, powerful at that time; that the Veientes, pressed by Servius Tullius, were defeated but not tamed; that the reign of Tarquinius Superbus was taken up by the crime of the murder of his father-in-law, kept by cruelty to the citizens and lost by the outrage of the violation of Lucretia; and, among the vices at home, the virtues shining abroad, that is the strong towns in Latium taken by him, Ardea, Oricolum, Suessa and Pometia, and whatever he achieved against Gabii, whether by his own fraud, by his son's punishment or by Roman strength. But how great were the evils that the Romans endured through 243 years of that continuous domination of kings is shown not only by the expulsion of one king, but by their abjuring of the royal name and power. For if the pride of only one man had been at fault, he alone should have been driven out and the royal dignity kept for better men. So when the kings had been driven from the city, the Romans, thinking that they should take counsel for themselves rather than leave anyone to lord it over their liberty, created consuls: under whom, as if in the grown age of a growing state, it was exercised in bolder ventures.

So when the kings had been driven from the city, the Romans, thinking that they should take counsel for themselves rather than leave anyone to lord it over their liberty, created consuls: under whom, as if in the grown age of a growing state, it was exercised in bolder ventures.

blocks: In the 244th year after the founding of the city Brutus, the first consul among the Romans, strove not only to equal the first founder and king of Rome in parricide but even to surpass him. For he dragged before the assembly his two young sons and as many brothers of his wife, the young Vitellii, charged with a plan to recall the kings to the City, beat them with rods and struck them with the axe. Then he himself, in the war with the Veientes and the Tarquinienses, met Arruns, the son of Superbus, in battle, and fell dying together with him. Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, a most weighty supporter of the royal name, forcing Tarquin on them, terrified, shut in and besieged the anxious city for three continuous years. And unless Mucius, by his steadfast endurance in burning his hand, or the maiden Cloelia, by her admirable boldness in crossing the river, had moved the enemy, the Romans would surely have been compelled to suffer either captivity, overcome by the pressing enemy, or slavery, subjected to the king they had taken back. After this the Sabines, scraping together forces from everywhere, marched on Rome with great preparation for war. Struck with fear at this, the Romans created a dictator, whose authority and power should go before the consul's; and this was of the greatest benefit in that war then. There followed the secession of the plebs from the fathers when, while the dictator M. Valerius was conducting a levy of soldiers, the people, goaded by various wrongs, occupied the Sacred Mount in arms. What could be more dreadful than this ruin, when the body, cut off from the head, was planning the destruction of that through which it drew breath? And the Roman name would have been finished by an inward ruin, had not a timely reconciliation crept in before the secession knew itself. Besides those open disasters of wars, a hidden ruin pressed on and threatened, with a wretched sequence: for in the consulship of T. Geganius and P. Minucius the two very greatest abominations of all evils, famine and pestilence, seized the weary city. Battles ceased for a little, but deaths did not cease. The Etruscan Veientes, heavy enemies, rising in war with the forces of their neighbours joined to them, were met by the consuls M. Fabius and Cn. Manlius. There, after the oath by which the Romans had devoted themselves not to return to camp except after victory, the contest was so savage and the appearance of conquered and conquerors so alike that, when most of the army had been lost and the consul Manlius and the consular Fabius had been killed in the fight, the consul M. Fabius refused to accept the triumph offered to him by the senate, because mourning rather was owed for such great losses to the state. What bereavement that family of the Fabii, most glorious in number and strength, brought on the state by its fall, when it drew the war with the Veientes as its lot, the river that destroyed them and the gate that sent them out bear witness, with names infamous to this day. For when three hundred and six Fabii, truly the brightest lights of the Roman state, had asked that a war against the Veientes be decreed to them as their own, they strengthened the hope of an expedition rashly undertaken by its first successes; then, drawn into an ambush and surrounded by the enemy, all were massacred there, only one being kept to announce the disaster, so that their country should hear more wretchedly that they were lost than it had lost them. Besides this, such things were not done at Rome only, but every province seethed with its own fires; and what the foremost poet described of one city, I would say of the whole world: "Everywhere cruel grief, everywhere fear, and very many an image of death."

blocks: At the same time, then, Cyrus, king of the Persians (whom I mentioned above for the sake of setting out the history, and who was then roaming with arms through Asia, Scythia and the whole east, while Tarquinius Superbus, as king or as enemy, was pressing the city either with slavery or with war): Cyrus, I say, having subdued all those against whom he had gone, made for the Assyrians and Babylon, then a people and a city wealthier than all. But the river Gyndes, second in size after the Euphrates, cut off his attack. For one of the royal horses, outstanding in whiteness and form, persuaded by confidence to cross, was snatched away, hurled down and drowned by the whirlpools that rose where they struck a shallow in the rushing bed. The king in his anger resolved to take vengeance on the river, declaring that the river that had now swallowed his splendid horse should be left fordable by women barely wetting their knees. Nor was he slower in carrying it out: with all his forces, for a whole year, he cut the river Gyndes through and drew it off into great ditches, breaking it up into four hundred and sixty channels. Using the diggers well trained by this work, he also diverted the Euphrates, by far the strongest river, which flows through the middle of Babylonia. And so, with the fords made passable and parts of the bed lying open, he made a dry path, and took the city that it was almost incredible to mortals either could have been built by human work or could be destroyed by human valour. For many have recorded that Babylon was founded by the giant Nimrod and restored by Ninus or Semiramis. It was visible on every side on a level plain, a most pleasant site by nature, laid out in a square like a camp, with equal walls. The strength and size of its walls are scarcely credible to tell: fifty cubits in breadth and four times as much in height. Its circuit, moreover, ran round four hundred and eighty stades. The wall was made of baked brick bonded with bitumen poured between, and a ditch, open wide on the outside, flowed round it in place of a river. In the front of the walls were a hundred gates of bronze. And the breadth itself, at the top of the battlements, with the dwellings of the defenders set equally on each side, took swift four-horse chariots in the space between. The houses within, of fourfold dwellings, were wonderful in their threatening height. And yet that great Babylon, the first founded after the restoration of the human race, was now conquered, taken and overthrown with almost the least delay. Croesus, king of the Lydians, famous for his wealth, had come there then to help the Babylonians; defeated, he fled anxiously back to his kingdom. Cyrus, after he had invaded Babylon as an enemy, overthrown it as a victor and ordered it as a king, carried the war into Lydia, where he overcame without any trouble an army already terrified by the earlier battle. He even captured Croesus himself, and when he had captured him he granted him both his life and his patrimony.

There is no need at this point to enlarge on the unstable states of changeable things. For the capture of Babylon confirms that whatever is made by labour and hand slips and is consumed by age. As its empire was the first and the most powerful, so it also was the first to give way, so that, as if by a certain right of the succeeding age, the inheritance owed to its successors might be handed on, and they too would keep the same rule of handing it on. So at the very first attempts of the approaching Cyrus great Babylon fell, and vast Lydia; the widest arms of the east, with their head, fell in the campaign of one battle. And our people complain with unconsidering anxiety if that mass of the once most powerful Roman state now trembles, shaken more by the weakness of its own old age than by the strength of others.

blocks: So the same Cyrus, with the success of the time just past, made war on the Scythians. Queen Tamyris, who was then at the head of that people, though she could have prevented him from crossing the river Araxes, allowed him to cross: first because of her confidence in herself, and then because of the advantage of having the enemy shut in by the barrier of the river. So Cyrus, entering Scythia, measured out a camp far from the river he had crossed, and then by a trick abandoned it, furnished with wine and feasts, as if he had fled in terror. When she learned this the queen sent a third of her forces and her young son to pursue Cyrus. The barbarians, as if invited to a feast, were first conquered by drunkenness, and soon, when Cyrus returned, all were cut down together with the young man. Tamyris, having lost her army and her son, prepared to wash away the grief of a mother and of a queen with the blood of the enemy rather than with her own tears. She feigned distrust, in despair at the disaster inflicted, and by gradually giving way she drew the proud enemy into an ambush. There, with an ambush laid among the mountains, she destroyed two hundred thousand Persians together with the king himself, with this added to the wonder of the thing above all, that not even a messenger of so great a disaster survived. The queen ordered the head of Cyrus to be cut off and thrown into a skin filled with human blood, taunting him not like a woman: "Glut yourself," she said, "with the blood you thirsted for, of which you went on insatiable for thirty years."

blocks: In the 245th year from the founding of the city Darius obtained the kingdom by lot, some interval after Cyrus had been killed among the Scythians. For Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, reigned between them. He conquered Egypt, abominated the whole religion of Egypt, and put down its ceremonies and temples. After him the Magi too dared to creep into the kingdom under the name of the king whom they had killed; but they were soon caught and crushed. So Darius, one of those who had put down the boldness of the Magi with the sword, was made king by the consent of all. After he had recovered by war the Assyrians and Babylon, which were revolting from the kingdom of the Persians, he made war on Antyrus, king of the Scythians, chiefly for this reason: that he had not obtained the marriage he sought with his daughter. A great necessity, no doubt, that seven hundred thousand men should be exposed to the danger of death for the lust of one man. For he entered Scythia with an incredible preparation, with seven hundred thousand armed men; and since the enemy gave him no chance of a proper battle, and moreover tore apart the ends of his forces with sudden raids, fearing that his return might be denied him if the bridge over the river Hister were broken, he fled back in alarm, having lost eighty thousand fighting men; though he did not count this number of the lost among his losses, and he did not feel the loss of a force that scarcely anyone would have dared to aspire to have. From there he attacked and subdued Asia and Macedonia. He also overcame the Ionians in a naval encounter. Then he made an attack on the Athenians, and directed his arms against them, because they had helped the Ionians against him. When the Athenians learned that Darius was approaching, though they had asked the Lacedaemonians for help, yet when they had learned that the Persians were held back by the idleness of a four-day religious observance, seizing the hope from the occasion, with only ten thousand citizens drawn up and a thousand Plataeans as auxiliaries, they burst out on the plains of Marathon against six hundred thousand of the enemy. Miltiades was in command in that war. Relying on speed more than on valour, by a quick enough advance he closed with the enemy hand to hand before he could be driven back by an unhindered discharge of arrows. So great was the difference of fighting in that war that on one side there seemed to be men ready to kill, on the other cattle prepared to die. blocks: Xerxes, succeeding his father Darius in the kingdom, spent five years preparing the war against Greece that his father had undertaken. Demaratus the Lacedaemonian, who happened then to be in exile with Xerxes, betrayed it to his people by means of tablets first written on and then covered with wax. Xerxes is said to have had seven hundred thousand armed men from his kingdom and three hundred thousand from his auxiliaries, and also twelve hundred beaked ships and three thousand transports; so that it has rightly been recorded that for so unheard-of an army and so immense a fleet the rivers were scarcely enough for drinking, the lands scarcely enough for marching, the seas scarcely enough for sailing. This column, so incredible in our times, whose number it is now harder to establish than it was then to conquer, Leonidas, king of the Spartans, withstood with four thousand men in the narrows of Thermopylae. Xerxes, in contempt of the small number set against him, ordered battle to be joined and hands to be locked. Those whose kinsmen and comrades had fallen on the plains of Marathon were the beginning both of the contest and of the disaster. Then, as a greater and slower crowd came on in turn, since it was now neither free to run forward nor unhindered to fight nor quick to flee, and was held up only by deaths, there was for three days on end not a battle of two peoples but the slaughter of one. On the fourth day, when Leonidas saw that the enemy was pouring round on every side, he urged his allied auxiliaries to withdraw from the battle, escape to the top of the mountain and keep themselves for better times; but he said that he and his Spartans must meet another lot: he owed more to his country than to his life. When he had sent the allies away he told the Spartans that they must hope for very much glory and nothing for life; that they must not wait either for the enemy or for daylight, but by the opportunity of night they must burst into the camp, mingle their arms with the enemy's and throw their columns into confusion; nowhere would the victors perish more honourably than in the camp of the enemy. So, persuaded to prefer to die, they armed for vengeance for their coming death, as though they both demanded and avenged their own destruction. Wonderful to tell, six hundred men burst into the camp of six hundred thousand. An uproar arose throughout the camp; the Persians themselves helped the Spartans by slaughtering one another; the Spartans, searching for the king and not finding him, cut down and laid low everything, roamed through the whole camp, and among the dense heaps of bodies could scarcely keep up with the few men left: victors beyond doubt, had they not chosen to die. The battle was drawn out from the beginning of the night into the greater part of the day. blocks: Xerxes, twice defeated on land, prepared a naval battle. But Themistocles, the leader of the Athenians, when he understood that the Ionians (in giving help to whom in the earlier war he had turned the attack of the Persians on himself) were bringing a fleet equipped to help Xerxes, determined to win them to his side and draw them away from the enemy. And because the opportunity of speaking with them was denied, he ordered signs to be set up and fixed on rocks in the places where the Ionians seemed likely to come with their ships. In them he rebuked with fitting reproach those who had once been allies and sharers in danger, but now were unjustly idle, and persuaded them with a religious exhortation to the rights of their ancient treaties, and warned them above all that, when battle was joined, they should back water like men giving way and take themselves out of the fighting. So the king, keeping part of the ships with him, stayed on the shore as a spectator of the battle. But Artemidora, queen of Halicarnassus, who had come to help Xerxes, threw herself into the fighting most fiercely among the foremost leaders, so that, the other way round, a woman's caution was seen in the man and a man's boldness in the woman. When the fight was doubtful the Ionians, following the instruction of Themistocles, began little by little to withdraw from the contest; and their defection persuaded the Persians, who were already looking round for flight, to flee openly. In this panic many ships were sunk and captured; but more, fearing the savagery of the king as much as the cruelty of the enemy, slipped away to their homes. text: Xerxes, twice defeated on land, prepared a naval battle. But Themistocles, the leader of the Athenians, when he understood that the Ionians (in giving help to whom in the earlier war he had turned the attack of the Persians on himself) were bringing a fleet equipped to help Xerxes, determined to win them to his side and draw them away from the enemy. blocks: But Mardonius, to whom Xerxes had entrusted the rest of the war, was first puffed up by a brief success and soon thrown down to the depths. He stormed Olynthus, a town of Greece. Having tried to lead the Athenians into a hope of peace by various solicitations, when he saw that their liberty could not be stormed, he burned part of the city and led all his equipment of war down into Boeotia. They took his camp, stuffed with the king's wealth, at no small cost indeed to their ancient industry: for after the division of this booty, Persian gold was the first corruption of the valour of Greece. Utter destruction, once begun, pressed on the wretched. For it happened that on the same day on which the forces of Mardonius were destroyed in Boeotia, part of the Persian army was fighting a naval battle in Asia under Mount Mycale. There a new rumour suddenly filled the ears of both fleets and peoples: that the forces of Mardonius had been wiped out and that the Greeks had been the victors. A wonderful ordering of divine judgement, that a battle fought in Boeotia at sunrise should be reported in Asia at midday on the same day, with such great spaces of sea and land lying between! This rumour supported above all the outcome that it made the Persians, seized on hearing of the disaster of their allies first with grief and then with despair, neither ready for battle nor fit for flight. And so the enemy, made more steadfast by his success, attacked them while they were dismayed and routed. Xerxes, having become contemptible to his people by waging the war in Greece unsuccessfully, was trapped in the palace by his prefect Artabanus and killed.

O times most worthy of longing and remembrance! O those days of unbroken calm, which are set before us to look back to as if out of darkness! In which, within the shortest interval, three wars under the three successive kings snatched nineteen hundred thousand men from the vitals of one kingdom; to say nothing of most unhappy Greece at that time, which surpassed in dying the whole number about which we now grow dull. That most famous Leonidas of the Lacedaemonians, in this war against Xerxes, which was the last both for himself and for the enemy, when he had spoken to his six hundred those most famous words of encouragement, "Take your breakfast as men who will dine among the dead", nevertheless advised the auxiliaries, whom he ordered to leave the war, mercifully, to keep themselves for better times. See, while he promised that the future would be better, these assert that the past was better: and when each loathes his own present, what else can be concluded but that the times are either always good but unthanked, or never better at all?

blocks: But at Rome (to return to the time from which I digressed; for I am not forced by the interval of miseries to pass to others, but, just as the evils boiling up everywhere were once bound together by their very deeds, so they are told mixed together; for our purpose is to compare the times of the world with one another, not to insult the labours of any part of it): at Rome, then, in the 290th year after the founding of the city, when war was halted for a little, a heavy pestilence, which there always either cut short the rare truces that had been made or forced them to be made, blazed up violently through the whole city; so that it was rightly with a prodigy going before that the sky seemed to be on fire, when the head of the nations burned with so great a fire of disease. For in that year the pestilence carried off both consuls, Aebutius and Servilius, wasted the military forces for the most part, and destroyed many nobles and above all the plebs with a foul wasting; though already four years before a plague had arisen and ravaged the same people.

Then in the next year exiled citizens and runaway slaves, led by Herbonius, a Sabine, seized and set fire to the Capitol. There the younger men resisted most bravely indeed under the consul and commander Valerius; but the crisis of the battle was so savage and heavy that the consul Valerius himself was killed there, and moreover defiled with his own death an unworthy victory over slaves.

There followed a year in which a consul was besieged with his defeated army. For the Aequi and Volsci overcame the consul Minucius when he met them in battle, and surrounded him as he fled on Algidus with hunger and the sword; and it would have ended unhappily had not Quinctius Cincinnatus, that outstanding dictator, crushed the enemy and broken the tight siege. Found in the country and summoned from the plough to the fasces, he took up the office, drew up an army and was soon made victor; he put the yoke of oxen on the Aequi, and, holding victory as if it were the plough handle, he drove the subjugated enemies before him, the first to do so.

blocks: In the year next to the three hundredth from the founding of the city, while the envoys sent to the Athenians to bring over the laws of Solon were awaited, famine and pestilence held Roman arms in check.

In the three hundredth year itself, that is in the ninety-fifth Olympiad, the power of the consuls, handed over to the decemvirs for the sake of drawing up laws on the Attic model, brought great ruin on the state. For first of the decemvirs, the rest giving way, Appius Claudius alone prolonged his command for himself, and at once a conspiracy of the others followed, so that, scorning the custom by which the insignia of command were with one man and the power was shared, all did everything at their own pleasure. So, among the other things that all of them most insolently presumed to do, suddenly each one came out with twelve fasces and the other insignia of command: and in this new beginning of a wicked ordering, with the religious respect for the consuls put away, a band of tyrants shone forth. Having added two tables of laws to the ten earlier ones, and doing very many things with most insolent arrogance, on the day on which it was the custom to lay down the magistracy they came out with the same insignia. The lust of Appius Claudius too increased their unpopularity greatly. In order to rape the maiden Verginia he first brought a suit claiming her as a slave; and so her father Verginius, driven by grief for her freedom and shame at the disgrace, in the sight of the people struck down his daughter, dragged off into slavery, a pious parricide. The people, moved by the cruelty of this necessity and warned of the danger to their liberty, occupied the Aventine Hill in arms. Nor did they stop defending their liberty with arms until the conspiracy of the plotters had abdicated their very offices too.

In the 103rd and 105th Olympiad, for almost the whole year, there were such frequent and such heavy earthquakes in Italy that Rome was wearied by continual news of countless shakings and collapses of villas and towns. Then there was so continuous and scorching a drought that it denied the hope of the earth bearing its fruits both for that year and for the next. In the same times, when the enemy Fidenates, terrible with a band of very great auxiliaries crowding round them, were threatening the citadels of the Romans, Aemilius, dictator for the third time, drove off and healed the great mass of evil, only just taking Fidena itself. Such was the strain of evils and of spirits among them that either the wars flooding in from outside blotted out the disasters at home, or, after the losses of wars, various plagues, blazing up from sky and earth, corrupted the truces they had relaxed with unceasing assault.

blocks: Sicily was from the beginning the homeland of the Cyclopes, and after them always the nurse of tyrants, often too the captive of slaves: of whom the first fed on the flesh of men, the middle ones on tortures, the last on deaths; except that in foreign wars it was held either as booty or as prize. To finish as briefly as possible, it knows no rest from evils except now; or rather, so that the differences of the times may be shown more plainly, as before it alone among all always suffered disorders internal or external, so now alone of all it never does. For even (to say nothing of the length either of that disaster by which it was pressed, or, on the contrary, of this peace which it enjoys) Etna itself, which then seethed with frequent eruptions, to the destruction of cities and fields, now only smokes with a harmless appearance, as proof of the past. So (to pass over for the present the tyrants, of whom whoever was the avenger was soon made the successor) in the meantime, that is in the 335th year from the founding of the city, when the people of Rhegium near Sicily were troubled by discord and the city was divided by dissension into two parts, one part called in veterans from Himera, a city of Sicily, to help them. Those veterans, having first driven out of the city those against whom they had been called in, and then soon slaughtered also those whom they had come to help, occupied the city with the wives and children of their allies, daring a crime that no tyrant could match. For it would have been better for the people of Rhegium to suffer anything rather than of their own accord invite men to whom they themselves, as exiles, would leave their country, wives, children and household gods as booty.

The people of Catina too, when they were suffering from the hostile and heavy Syracusans, asked the Athenians for help. But the Athenians, more for their own interest than for that of their allies, sent a fleet equipped to Sicily, since they were both planning to extend their empire and feared that the Syracusan fleet, newly equipped, would help the Lacedaemonians. And because the Athenians who had been sent had made a prosperous beginning by slaughtering the enemy, they brought back larger forces and a stronger army into Sicily under the generals Laches and Chariades. But the people of Catina, moved by weariness of the war, made a treaty with the Syracusans and spurned the help of the Athenians. Afterwards, however, when the Syracusans, intent on domination, overstepped the terms of peace, they again sent envoys to Athens, unkempt in hair and beard and dressed in mourning, to beg for pity and help by both speech and dress. So a great fleet was equipped under the generals Nicias and Lamachus, and Sicily was sought again with such great forces that even those who had obtained the vote feared it. The Athenians at once fought two infantry battles with favourable success, and shut in the enemy, worn down in the city and surrounded by the fleet set against them, by land and sea. But the Syracusans, with their affairs broken and wearied, asked the Lacedaemonians for help. Gylippus was soon sent by them, alone indeed, but one who was put forward as the equal of all reinforcements. On arriving, when he heard that the state of the war was already sinking, he gathered auxiliaries partly in Greece and partly in Sicily and seized places favourable for the war. Then, defeated in two battles but not frightened, in the third encounter he killed Lamachus, put the enemy to flight and freed his allies from the siege. From here the Athenians, defeated in a land battle, made trial of the sea and prepared to engage in a naval contest. When Gylippus learned this he sent for an equipped fleet from the Lacedaemonians; the Athenians likewise sent Demosthenes and Eurymedon, with fresh forces, in place of the lost general; and the Peloponnesians too, by the consent and decree of many cities, sent great help to the Syracusans. So, under the appearance of a war for allies, they carried on their domestic quarrels, and, as if the contest had by agreement been transferred from Greece to Sicily, they fought on both sides with their utmost strength. So the Athenians were beaten in the first encounter, and lost their camp too with all their money, public and private, and the whole equipment of a long campaign. With their resources broken and reduced to straits, Demosthenes urged that, while their affairs were not yet wholly lost, however battered they seemed, they should return home and leave Sicily; but Nicias, made more desperate by shame at things badly managed from the beginning, insisted on staying. They renewed the naval contest and soon, through lack of skill, were drawn into the narrows of the sea of Syracuse and caught in the enemy's ambush: the general Eurylochus was killed first, and eleven ships were burned. Demosthenes and Nicias abandoned the fleet, as if they would flee more safely by a land march. But Gylippus first seized their hundred and thirty abandoned ships, and then, setting out to pursue the fugitives themselves, captured and killed a great many. Demosthenes escaped the disgrace of slavery by a voluntary death; but Nicias crowned an unworthy and shameful life with the disgrace of captivity.

blocks: So the Athenians, having struggled for two years in Sicily, not without loss to the Lacedaemonians, were beset by other evils at home. For Alcibiades, who had earlier been declared general against Syracuse, and was soon held for trial on some charge, went into voluntary exile to Lacedaemon and pushed the Spartans, while the Athenians were in disorder, to press on again with a new war and not to give them room to breathe before they were crushed. All Greece agreed to this undertaking as if, for the public good, counsel were being taken with combined forces to put out a common fire. Darius too, king of the Persians, remembering his father's and grandfather's hatred for this city, made a treaty with the Lacedaemonians through Tissaphernes, the prefect of Lydia, and promised them the costs of the war and forces. Wonderful to tell, so great was the strength of the Athenians at that time that, when they were attacked, that is a single city, by the forces of Greece, Asia and the whole east, they seem to have been worn out by often fighting and never giving way rather than conquered. For at first Alcibiades forced all their allies to revolt from them to the Lacedaemonians; but, attacked by the Lacedaemonians too with an ambush out of envy, he fled and withdrew to Tissaphernes. Having at once become more intimate with him by a ready wit and the charm of fitting eloquence, he persuaded him not to help the Lacedaemonians with such lavish wealth; he ought rather to become the umpire and spectator of this contest, and to keep the strength of Lydia intact against the victor. For this reason Tissaphernes ordered part of the fleet, with a considerable force, to be taken to Lacedaemon, so that the Lacedaemonians should neither fight safely at another's risk with abundant support, nor, wholly abandoned, give up the contest they had undertaken.

So the thirty governors appointed for the Athenians rose up as thirty tyrants. First they surrounded themselves with three thousand attendants, and soon they also set seven hundred soldiers of the victorious army about their persons. They made the killing of Alcibiades the omen of a slaughter of all, everywhere, to come: as he fled he was shut in a bedroom on the road and burned alive. When he had been killed, secure as if the avenger had been removed, they drained the wretched remnants of the city with slaughter and plunder. That battle was savage; but since the one side was fighting for the liberty of its country, the other for domination over another's, the fight itself gave judgement on their spirits and causes. Then, when battle had been declared and they first came together as if for a parley, the tyrants were trapped in an ambush and massacred like victims of peace. So, called back into one, after the insatiable tears of great joys, they laid these first foundations of their recovered liberty, with the solemn testimony of an oath that the discords and animosities of the past should be brought into perpetual oblivion and undying silence. A most wise provision of the Athenians, especially after so many proofs of miseries: if only human affairs could prevail, with the consent of men lasting, as they are ordered. Yet the Athenians, wisest of all, and taught well enough by their own evils that the smallest things grow by concord and the greatest fall by discord, and that all things, good or even evil, that are done abroad are rooted in and sent out from inward beginnings, wiped away hatreds at home and suppressed wars abroad, and left their descendants an example from their ruin and a counsel from their restoration: if only, because of the weakest changeableness of the human mind, what is counselled in adversity were kept in prosperity.

Yet these very things, because they have faded through the long interval of ages, have become for us exercises for the wit and the delights of stories. Let anyone dare, if he can, to compare any disturbances of this time with that disaster: though the story of a past evil does not weigh as much as the injury of a present one. So the Senonian Gauls, under the leadership of Brennus, with a numerous and very strong army, while they were besieging the city of Clusium, which is now called Tuscia, saw the envoys of the Romans, who had come then to make peace between them, fighting against them in the battle line. Moved with indignation at this, they gave up the siege of the town of Clusium and made for Rome with all their strength. As they rushed on in this way the consul Fabius met them with an army; but he did not withstand them; rather, that hostile charge cut down, laid low and passed over it like a dry crop. The river Allia bears witness to this disaster of Fabius, as the Cremera does to that of the Fabii. For no one could easily recount a like ruin of the Roman soldiery, even had Rome not been burned besides. The Gauls entered the open city; they massacred the senators sitting stiff like statues in their seats, and, burning them in the fire of their houses, buried them under the fall of their own roofs. All the rest of the youth, which is known to have been barely a thousand men at that time, hiding in the citadel of the Capitoline Hill, they shut in by a siege, and there they wore down, subdued and sold the unhappy remnants by hunger, plague, despair and dread: for they agreed on a thousand pounds of gold as the price of their departure; not that Rome was of small name among the Gauls, but that they had already worn it down so much before that it could not then be worth more. When the Gauls went out there remained, in that former circuit of the city, a foul heap of shapeless ruins; and everywhere, as people wandered through the obstructions and did not know one another among their own homes, the echo of a voice that struck against them, answering, held their frightened hearing in suspense. Horror shook their minds, the very silences terrified them, since rarity in wide spaces is the stuff of fear. Hence they thought of, agreed upon and attempted changing their dwelling place, living in another town, and even being registered under another name.

Behold the times by comparison with which the present are weighed; behold the times for which remembrance sighs; behold the times that strike repentance for the religion chosen, or rather neglected! Truly these two captivities are equal and are compared with each other: the one raging for six months and this one passing in three days; the Gauls, when the people had been wiped out and the city destroyed, pursuing the very name of Rome to its last ashes, and the Goths, giving up their intention of plundering, driving bewildered crowds to the refuges of safety, that is to the holy places; there scarcely any senator found who escaped even by being absent, here scarcely anyone sought who perhaps perished in hiding. I might rightly compare that the number of the saved there was the number of the lost here. Plainly, as the facts show, it must be confessed too: in this present disaster God raged more and men less, since, by Himself doing what they had not completed, He showed why He had sent them. And since the matter for speaking is abundant and can by no means be concluded in this book, let this be the end of the present volume, so that we may pursue the rest in those that follow.

blocks: In the 944th year from the founding of the city Severus, an African by birth, a Tripolitanian from the town of Lepcis, who wished to be called Pertinax after the name of the emperor whose murder he had avenged, seventeenth from Augustus, obtained the empire, which had been left without a ruler, and held it eighteen years. Savage by nature and always harried by many wars, he ruled the state very bravely indeed, but with very great toil. He defeated and killed at Cyzicus Pescennius Niger, who had aspired to tyranny in Egypt and Syria. He put down with the sword the Jews and Samaritans when they tried to rebel. He overcame the Parthians, the Arabs and the Adiabeni. In the fifth persecution after Nero he tortured the Christians, and a great many of the saints in various provinces were crowned with martyrdom. This profane presumption of Severus against the Christians and the Church of God was followed at once by the vengeance of heaven. For immediately Severus was snatched, or rather dragged back, from Syria into Gaul to a third civil war. He had already waged one at Rome against Julianus, and another in Syria against Pescennius; the third was stirred up by Clodius Albinus, Julianus's partner in the killing of Pertinax, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul. In this war much Roman blood was shed on both sides. Albinus, however, was crushed and killed near Lugdunum. Severus, the victor, was drawn into the Britains by the defection of almost all the allies. There, after fighting many great and heavy battles, he decided to separate the part of the island he had recovered from the other, unconquered peoples by a wall. So he drew a great ditch and a very strong rampart, fortified besides with frequent towers, for one hundred and thirty-two miles from sea to sea. And there, at the town of Eboracum, he died of illness. He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta. Of these Geta was judged a public enemy and perished; Bassianus took the surname Antoninus and gained the throne.

Savage by nature and always harried by many wars, he ruled the state very bravely indeed, but with very great toil. He defeated and killed at Cyzicus Pescennius Niger, who had aspired to tyranny in Egypt and Syria. He put down with the sword the Jews and Samaritans when they tried to rebel. He overcame the Parthians, the Arabs and the Adiabeni. In the fifth persecution after Nero he tortured the Christians, and a great many of the saints in various provinces were crowned with martyrdom. This profane presumption of Severus against the Christians and the Church of God was followed at once by the vengeance of heaven. For immediately Severus was snatched, or rather dragged back, from Syria into Gaul to a third civil war. He had already waged one at Rome against Julianus, and another in Syria against Pescennius; the third was stirred up by Clodius Albinus, Julianus's partner in the killing of Pertinax, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul. In this war much Roman blood was shed on both sides. Albinus, however, was crushed and killed near Lugdunum. Severus, the victor, was drawn into the Britains by the defection of almost all the allies. There, after fighting many great and heavy battles, he decided to separate the part of the island he had recovered from the other, unconquered peoples by a wall. So he drew a great ditch and a very strong rampart, fortified besides with frequent towers, for one hundred and thirty-two miles from sea to sea. And there, at the town of Eboracum, he died of illness. He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta. Of these Geta was judged a public enemy and perished; Bassianus took the surname Antoninus and gained the throne.

blocks: In the 962nd year from the founding of the city Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus, also called Caracalla, eighteenth from Augustus, obtained the principate and remained in it not quite seven years. He lived more harshly than his father, and more intemperate in lust than any man, for he even married his stepmother Julia. While he was preparing war against the Parthians he was surrounded by the enemy between Edessa and Carrhae and killed.

After him Opilius Macrinus, nineteenth from Augustus, who was praetorian prefect, seized the empire with his son Diadumenus, but when a year had passed he was at once killed at Archelais in a mutiny of the soldiers.

In the 970th year from the founding of the city Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, twentieth from Augustus, obtained the empire and held it four years. This priest of the temple of Heliogabalus left no memory of himself but one infamous enough for debauchery, outrages and every obscenity. When a mutiny of the soldiers broke out, he was killed at Rome together with his mother.

In the 974th year from the founding of the city Aurelius Alexander, twenty-first from Augustus, was made emperor by the will of the senate and the soldiers, and for thirteen years he deserved the praise of justice. His mother Mamaea, a Christian, took care to hear the presbyter Origen. For at once, making an expedition against the Persians, he overwhelmed their king Xerxes, victor in a very great war. Using Ulpian as his assessor, he showed the state the greatest moderation; but he was killed at Mogontiacum in a mutiny of the soldiers.

blocks: In the 987th year from the founding of the city Maximinus, twenty-second from Augustus, was made emperor by the army without any will of the senate, after he had waged a successful war in Germany, and carried out a persecution of the Christians, the sixth from Nero. But at once, that is in the third year of his reign, he was killed by Pupienus at Aquileia and made an end of both his persecution and his life. He had launched the persecution against the priests and clergy, that is the teachers, chiefly because of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he had succeeded, and of his mother Mamaea, and above all because of the presbyter Origen.

In the 991st year from the founding of the city Gordian, twenty-third from Augustus, was made emperor and remained in it six years. For Pupienus, the killer of Maximinus, and his brother Balbinus, who had usurped the empire, were soon killed in the Palace. Gordian, still quite a boy, about to set out to the east for the Parthian war, opened the gates of Janus, as Eutropius writes. Whether anyone closed them after Vespasian and Titus I do not remember anyone having written, although Cornelius Tacitus records that they were opened by Vespasian himself a year later. So Gordian, after fighting great battles successfully against the Parthians, was killed through the treachery of his own men not far from Circesium, above the Euphrates.

blocks: In the 997th year from the founding of the city Philip, twenty-fourth from Augustus, was made emperor, made his son Philip his partner in the rule, and remained in it seven years. He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian, and after the third year of his reign the thousandth year from the founding of Rome was completed. So this birthday year, the most august of all that had gone before, was celebrated with magnificent games by a Christian emperor. Nor is there any doubt that Philip referred the thanks and honour for so great a devotion to Christ and the Church, since no writer shows either that there was a procession up to the Capitol or that victims were sacrificed according to custom. Both, however, though in different places, were killed in a mutiny of the soldiers and by the treachery of Decius.

blocks: In the 1004th year from the founding of the city Decius, the instigator and the suppressor of a civil war, when the Philips had been killed, seized the empire, twenty-fifth from Augustus, and held it three years. He at once, to show that he had killed Philip for this reason too, sent out deadly edicts for the persecution and killing of the Christians, seventh after Nero, and sent a great many of the saints from their crosses to the crowns of Christ. He also chose his son as Caesar, and was killed together with him at once, in the very midst of the barbarians.

In the 1007th year from the founding of the city Gallus Hostilianus, twenty-sixth from Augustus, obtained the throne and held it with his son Volusianus for barely two years. The vengeance for the violated name of Christian breaks out, and as far as the edicts of Decius had run for the ruin of the churches, so far the plague of unbelievable diseases spreads. There was scarcely a Roman province, scarcely a city, scarcely a house that was not seized and emptied by that general pestilence. Gallus and Volusianus, notable for this disaster alone, were killed while they were preparing a civil war against Aemilianus, who was planning revolution. Aemilianus, however, was dead in the third month of the tyranny he had seized.

blocks: In the 1010th year from the founding of the city two emperors were made in the twenty-seventh place after Augustus: Valerian was hailed Augustus by the army in Raetia, while at Rome Gallienus was made Caesar by the senate. Gallienus remained on the throne unhappily for fifteen years, while the human race breathed again for a little from that pestilence, more continuous and heavier than usual. Forgetful malice provokes its own punishment. For impiety, when it is scourged, feels the lashes indeed, but hardened, it does not feel by whom it is scourged. To say nothing of earlier times, when Decius had made his persecution of the Christians, a great pestilence afflicted the whole Roman Empire. Wickedness lied to itself, caught by its own crooked judgement to its ruin, that the pestilence was a common chance, and that death from disease was the end set by nature and not a punishment. So once again, and in a short time, it provokes the anger of God by wicked deeds, about to receive a blow that it would be forced to remember for some while. For Valerian, eighth from Nero, as soon as he had seized the empire, ordered Christians to be forced by torture into idolatry and those who refused to be killed, and the blood of the saints was shed through the whole breadth of the Roman realm. At once Valerian, the author of the wicked edict, was captured by Shapur, king of the Persians, and the emperor of the Roman people grew old among the Persians in a most shameful slavery. As long as he lived he was condemned to this continual degrading office: bending to the ground, he always raised the king when he was about to mount his horse, not with his hand but with his back. And Gallienus, frightened by so clear a judgement of God and shaken by the wretched example of his colleague, restored peace to the churches with anxious amends. But the captivity of one impious man, however lasting and however beyond measure abominable, does not make up the full measure of the wrong and of the vengeance for so many thousands of saints tortured; and the blood of the righteous, crying to God, asks to be avenged in the same land where it was shed. For it was not of the maker of the order alone that punishment was demanded by just judgement, but it was just that the executors, informers, accusers, spectators and judges, and last of all everyone who assented to that most unjust cruelty even by silent goodwill (for God knows what is hidden), should be struck by the same blow of vengeance; and these were the greater part of mankind, in every province. Suddenly, by God's leave, the peoples who had been placed round about and left for this purpose are let loose on every side, and with the reins slackened they burst into all the territories of the Romans. The Germans pass through the Alps, Raetia and all Italy and come as far as Ravenna; the Alamanni roam through the Gauls and cross into Italy as well; Greece, Macedonia, Pontus and Asia are wiped out by a flood of Goths; for Dacia beyond the Danube is taken away for ever; the Quadi and Sarmatians lay waste the Pannonias; the farther Germans strip Spain and take possession of it; the Parthians take away Mesopotamia and scrape Syria bare. There still stand in various provinces, among the ruins of great cities, small and poor dwellings that keep the signs of the miseries and the evidence of the names; among them we too can show our own Tarraco in Spain, for consolation in a recent misery. And so that no part of the Roman body should be spared this tearing apart, tyrants conspire within, civil wars arise, and a great deal of Roman blood is shed everywhere, as Romans and barbarians rage. But soon the anger of God is turned to mercy, and the vengeance begun is reckoned more as a warning than as a punishment in its full measure. So first Genuus, who had taken up the purple of empire, is killed at Mursa. Postumus seized tyranny in Gaul, to the great benefit of the state indeed: for ten years, using great courage and moderation, he both drove out the enemies who were lording it and restored the lost provinces to their former appearance; he was, however, killed in a mutiny of the soldiers. Aemilianus was crushed at Mogontiacum when he was plotting revolution. After the death of Postumus, Marius seized the empire in the same place but was at once killed. Then Victorinus was made emperor by the Gauls of their own accord and was killed after a little while. He was succeeded by Tetricus, who was then governing as praeses of Aquitania. He endured many mutinies of the soldiers. But in the east, by a certain Odenathus, who gathered a band of countrymen, the Persians were defeated and driven back, Syria was defended and Mesopotamia recovered, and the countrymen of Syria, with their Odenathus, came conquering as far as Ctesiphon. Gallienus, however, when he had abandoned the state and was a slave to his lusts at Mediolanum, was killed.

blocks: In the 1025th year from the founding of the city Claudius, twenty-eighth, took up the empire by the will of the senate, and at once attacked the Goths, who had been laying waste Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years already, and destroyed them with incredible slaughter. The senate decreed him a golden shield in the senate house and an equally golden statue on the Capitol; but at once, at Sirmium, before he had completed two years in the empire, he was seized by illness and died.

When Claudius was dead his brother Quintillus was chosen emperor by the army, a man of unique moderation and the only one to be preferred to his brother; he was killed on the seventeenth day of his reign.

In the 1027th year from the founding of the city Aurelian, twenty-ninth, obtained the empire and held it five years and six months, a man most excellent in military energy. Taking up an expedition to the Danube, he routed the Goths in great battles and established Roman sway at its ancient boundaries. Then, turning to the east, he brought under his power Zenobia, who after the killing of her husband Odenathus was claiming for herself the Syria he had recovered, more by the terror of battle than by battle. Tetricus, who in Gaul was quite unable to withstand the mutinies of his soldiers and was even writing, "Rescue me, unconquered one, from these evils", and so was the betrayer of his own army, he overcame without effort. So, the recoverer of the east and the north, he celebrated a triumph with great glory. He surrounded the city of Rome with stronger walls. At the last, when he was decreeing a persecution against the Christians, ninth from Nero, a thunderbolt fell before him, to the great terror of those standing about, and not long after he was killed on a journey.

blocks: In the 1032nd year from the founding of the city Tacitus, thirtieth, obtained the empire and was killed in Pontus in the sixth month. After him Florianus, who had an equal lot in the rule, was killed at Tarsus in only the third month.

In the 1033rd year from the founding of the city Probus, thirty-first, obtained the throne and held it six years and four months. Through many heavy battles, the enemies at last destroyed, he completely freed the Gauls, which had long been occupied by barbarians. Then he waged two civil wars, with a great deal of blood: one in the east, in which he crushed and captured Saturninus, who was relying on a tyranny; the other in which he defeated Proculus and Bonosus in great battles at Agrippina and killed them. He himself, however, was killed at Sirmium in an iron tower in a mutiny of the soldiers.

In the 1039th year from the founding of the city Carus of Narbo, thirty-second, took up the empire and held it two years. When he had made his sons Carinus and Numerian partners in the rule, in the Parthian war, after he had taken Coche and Ctesiphon, two very famous cities of the Parthians, he was struck by lightning in his camp above the Tigris and died. Numerian, who had been with his father, was killed on the way back through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper.

blocks: In the 1041st year from the founding of the city Diocletian, thirty-third, was chosen emperor by the army and was emperor twenty years. As soon as he had the means of power he killed with his own hand Aper, the killer of Numerian. Then, in a very difficult war and with very great toil, he overcame Carinus, whom Carus had left as Caesar in Dalmatia, and who was living shamefully. Next, when in Gaul Amandus and Aelianus had gathered a band of country people, whom they called Bacaudae, and stirred up destructive disorders, he made Maximian, surnamed Herculius, Caesar and sent him into the Gauls; and he easily settled the unskilled and disorderly band of rustics with military valour. Then a certain Carausius, of the lowest birth indeed but quick in counsel and in action, had been posted to watch the shores of the Ocean, which the Franks and Saxons were then infesting. He was acting more to the ruin than to the advancement of the state: the booty he took from the pirates he gave back in no part to its owners but claimed for himself alone, and so he roused the suspicion that he was letting the enemies themselves raid the frontiers by a crafty negligence. When for this reason Maximian ordered him to be killed, he took up the purple and seized the Britains. So the crash of sudden disorders sounded through all the frontiers of the Roman Empire: Carausius was rebelling in the Britains, Achilleus in Egypt, while the Quinquegentiani were harassing Africa, and Narseh too, king of the Persians, was pressing the east with war. Disturbed by this danger, Diocletian made Maximian Herculius Augustus from Caesar, and chose Constantius and Maximian Galerius as Caesars. Constantius took as his wife Theodora, the stepdaughter of Maximian Herculius, and by her had six sons, the brothers of Constantine. Carausius, after claiming and holding Britain for himself very bravely for seven years, was at last killed through the treachery of his partner Allectus. Allectus afterwards held for three years the island he had taken from Carausius. Asclepiodotus, the praetorian prefect, crushed him and recovered Britain after ten years. Constantius Caesar, in Gaul, when his army was routed by the Alamanni in the first battle, was himself barely snatched away; but in the second a quite favourable victory followed, for sixty thousand Alamanni are reported to have been cut down in a few hours. And Maximian Augustus tamed the Quinquegentiani in Africa. Then, too, Diocletian besieged Achilleus at Alexandria for eight months, took him and killed him. But using his victory without restraint, he gave Alexandria over to plunder and defiled all Egypt with proscriptions and killings. Besides, Galerius Maximian, when he had already fought two battles against Narseh, met him a third time between Callinicum and Carrhae and was defeated; having lost his forces, he fled back to Diocletian. Diocletian received him most arrogantly, so that he is said to have run for some miles in his purple before his carriage. Yet he used this insult as a whetstone for courage: by it the rust of royal pride was rubbed away and he sharpened the edge of his mind. So he soon gathered forces from all over Illyricum and Moesia, swiftly returned against the enemy and overcame Narseh with great strategy and strength. When the forces of the Persians had been destroyed and Narseh himself put to flight, he attacked his camp, captured his wives, sisters and children, plundered an immense quantity of Persian treasure, and led away a great many captives from among the Persian nobles. Returning to Mesopotamia he was received by Diocletian with the greatest honour. Afterwards the same commanders fought vigorously against the Carpi and the Bastarnae. Then they defeated the Sarmatians, and a very great multitude of captives from them they scattered among the garrisons of the Roman frontiers.

Meanwhile Diocletian in the east and Maximian Herculius in the west ordered the churches to be laid waste and the Christians to be afflicted and killed, in the tenth place after Nero. This persecution was longer and more savage than almost all those carried out before, for for ten years it went on without ceasing, with the burning of churches, the proscription of the innocent and the killing of martyrs. There followed an earthquake in Syria, by which, as roofs fell everywhere at Tyre and Sidon, many thousands of people were crushed. In the second year of the persecution Diocletian required of Maximian, against his will, that they should lay down the purple and the empire together, and that, when younger men had been put in their place over the state, they themselves should grow old in private leisure. So on one day Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Mediolanum laid down together the power of empire and its trappings.

But Constantius, a most peaceable man, content with Gaul only [and Spain], gave up the other parts to Galerius. text: In the 1041st year from the founding of the city Diocletian, thirty-third, was chosen emperor by the army and was emperor twenty years. As soon as he had the means of power he killed with his own hand Aper, the killer of Numerian. Then, in a very difficult war and with very great toil, he overcame Carinus, whom Carus had left as Caesar in Dalmatia, and who was living shamefully. Next, when in Gaul Amandus and Aelianus had gathered a band of country people, whom they called Bacaudae, and stirred up destructive disorders, he made Maximian, surnamed Herculius, Caesar and sent him into the Gauls; and he easily settled the unskilled and disorderly band of rustics with military valour. Then a certain Carausius, of the lowest birth indeed but quick in counsel and in action, had been posted to watch the shores of the Ocean, which the Franks and Saxons were then infesting. He was acting more to the ruin than to the advancement of the state: the booty he took from the pirates he gave back in no part to its owners but claimed for himself alone, and so he roused the suspicion that he was letting the enemies themselves raid the frontiers by a crafty negligence. When for this reason Maximian ordered him to be killed, he took up the purple and seized the Britains. So the crash of sudden disorders sounded through all the frontiers of the Roman Empire: Carausius was rebelling in the Britains, Achilleus in Egypt, while the Quinquegentiani were harassing Africa, and Narseh too, king of the Persians, was pressing the east with war. Disturbed by this danger, Diocletian made Maximian Herculius Augustus from Caesar, and chose Constantius and Maximian Galerius as Caesars. Constantius took as his wife Theodora, the stepdaughter of Maximian Herculius, and by her had six sons, the brothers of Constantine. Carausius, after claiming and holding Britain for himself very bravely for seven years, was at last killed through the treachery of his partner Allectus. Allectus afterwards held for three years the island he had taken from Carausius. Asclepiodotus, the praetorian prefect, crushed him and recovered Britain after ten years. Constantius Caesar, in Gaul, when his army was routed by the Alamanni in the first battle, was himself barely snatched away; but in the second a quite favourable victory followed, for sixty thousand Alamanni are reported to have been cut down in a few hours. And Maximian Augustus tamed the Quinquegentiani in Africa. Then, too, Diocletian besieged Achilleus at Alexandria for eight months, took him and killed him. But using his victory without restraint, he gave Alexandria over to plunder and defiled all Egypt with proscriptions and killings. Besides, Galerius Maximian, when he had already fought two battles against Narseh, met him a third time between Callinicum and Carrhae and was defeated; having lost his forces, he fled back to Diocletian. Diocletian received him most arrogantly, so that he is said to have run for some miles in his purple before his carriage. Yet he used this insult as a whetstone for courage: by it the rust of royal pride was rubbed away and he sharpened the edge of his mind. So he soon gathered forces from all over Illyricum and Moesia, swiftly returned against the enemy and overcame Narseh with great strategy and strength. When the forces of the Persians had been destroyed and Narseh himself put to flight, he attacked his camp, captured his wives, sisters and children, plundered an immense quantity of Persian treasure, and led away a great many captives from among the Persian nobles. Returning to Mesopotamia he was received by Diocletian with the greatest honour. Afterwards the same commanders fought vigorously against the Carpi and the Bastarnae. Then they defeated the Sarmatians, and a very great multitude of captives from them they scattered among the garrisons of the Roman frontiers. Meanwhile Diocletian in the east and Maximian Herculius in the west ordered the churches to be laid waste and the Christians to be afflicted and killed, in the tenth place after Nero. This persecution was longer and more savage than almost all those carried out before, for for ten years it went on without ceasing, with the burning of churches, the proscription of the innocent and the killing of martyrs. There followed an earthquake in Syria, by which, as roofs fell everywhere at Tyre and Sidon, many thousands of people were crushed. In the second year of the persecution Diocletian required of Maximian, against his will, that they should lay down the purple and the empire together, and that, when younger men had been put in their place over the state, they themselves should grow old in private leisure.
